title: How to make McDonald's 'Grandma McFlurry': At-home recipe
fullText:
Are you a fan of butterscotch and nostalgia, but not of desserts made with unidentified ingredients and mystery "caramel-colored syrup"?

Then you're probably stuck in a little dilemma over whether or not to try McDonald's new Grandma McFlurry.

On the one hand, you'd love to savor vanilla ice cream infused with "the candies Grandma used to hide in her purse" (don't worry; they meant Werther's, not spearmint Life Savers).

But, on the other, you're not totally sold on the nameless goo they blend into it, or the fact that long term research on the effects of eating McDonald's corn syrup-y desserts has not yet been conducted.

Well, good news! You don't have to visit the Golden Arches to try the limited-edition cryptic treat.

With this simple DIY recipe, you can make the Grandma McFlurry — in whatever quality your tastebuds desire — right at home.

How to make McDonald's Grandma McFlurry at home

McDonald's McFlurrys are known for their creamy texture, in addition to the toppings blended into them. To recreate that thin consistency, then, you will need more than just ice cream.

And, as for the flavor of the Grandma version? "Syrup" and "crushed candies" give it a butterscotch taste.

Here's what you need to make both of those things happen.

Recipe to make McDonald's Grandma McFlurry at home

Ingredients:

  • 4 cups vanilla ice cream
  • 4 tablespoons milk (to thin the consistency)
  • 6 ounces Cool Whip (to create that light, airy texture)
  • Butterscotch syrup (we recommend a thick one, like Smucker's, before a barista-style one. If unavailable, caramel syrup suffices)
  • English Toffee Bits (Heath makes a bagged version of these that you can get on Amazon or at ACME, or you can pre-crush some toffee yourself)

Instructions:

  1. Add the ice cream, milk and Cool Whip to a blender and blend until smooth. *If you don't have a blender, use a mixer and a bowl.*
  2. Add in the butterscotch syrup and toffee pieces, mixing until you attain a light golden brown color. For a true McDonald's experience, you barely need to mix at all (lately, the chain has just been pouring the candy and syrup over the top, but we don't think that tastes so great).
  3. Pour into a cup and enjoy with a spoon.

Yield: 2 servings.

PS: If you want to spike this and make it boozy (Grandma is an adult, after all), we think it pairs best with rum.

Kara VanDooijeweert is a food writer for NorthJersey.com and The Record. If you can't find her in Jersey's best restaurants, she's probably off running a race course in the mountains. Catch her on Instagram: @karanicolev & @northjerseyeats, and sign up for her North Jersey Eats newsletter.

title: You can eat with celebrities at this star-studded New Jersey golf event
fullText:
What do Lee Trevino, Marcus Samuelsson and CC Sabathia have in common? All have been spotted at Alpine Country Club's Celebrity Chefs & Friends Golf and Tennis Tournament.

Held annually at North Jersey's most posh golf venue, the event — which is known more as being a "day camp" for top chefs than a cutthroat athletic competition — attracts all the region's biggest celebrities; from culinary icons to sports legends.

And, at the end of the evening? All of the proceeds are donated to New York's biggest food rescue organization, City Harvest, which helps deliver meals to people in need.

Here's everything we know about the upcoming "food and wine festival that happens to take place on a golf course" — and how you can get in on it.

A star-studded food festival on a lavish golf course

Celebrity Chefs & Friends Golf and Tennis Tournament is an all-day charity event during which golf foursomes (AKA, you guys) are joined by a fifth player (a chef, celebrity or sports personality) on the manicured grounds of Alpine Country Club. Tennis players will be accompanied by renowned chefs and restaurateurs.

This year's event will be held on Monday, June 24.

Throughout the afternoon, athletes will duke it out for the top titles on the court/course, with both tournaments culminating in a lavish reception — hosted by 65(+) celebrity chefs and acclaimed restaurants.

In other words? You don't need to know anything about sports to attend.

You just need a big appetite.

An exquisite reception for a worthy cause

The country club's annual tournament is always hosted by big names, who, this year, will be golf superstar Lee Trevino and tennis great Reilly Opelka.

Set to begin at 9:30 a.m., the day will open with the sports competitions, followed by the food reception at 5:30 p.m. Tickets can be purchased for both parts or (if you're more of a foodie, like most attendees) the reception only.

During the reception, guests will be treated to a luxurious spread of food and cocktails from New York City and Bergen County's top chefs and most highly decorated restaurants. In the past, gastronomic stars from Le Bernardin, Restaurant Daniel and COTE have attended, alongside Food Network personalities like Geoffrey Zakarian.

Some menu highlights have included soy-marinated short ribs, lamb lollipops and thousands of dollars of Snake River Farm steaks, to name a few.

So, if you have $1,000 to spare for a ticket — or you're willing to splurge in the name of once-in-a-lifetime eats and guaranteed celebrity elbow brushes — hurry up and grab your ticket; because the popular event is expected to sell out soon.

The Celebrity Chefs & Friends Golf and Tennis Tournament will be hosted at 80 Anderson Ave. in Demarest on Monday, June 24. Tickets can be purchased at ccfgtt24.eventlify.com.

Kara VanDooijeweert is a food writer for NorthJersey.com and The Record. If you can't find her in Jersey's best restaurants, she's probably off running a race course in the mountains. Catch her on Instagram: @karanicolev & @northjerseyeats, and sign up for her North Jersey Eats newsletter.

title: Tommy's Tavern+ Tap will open new location in Edgewater NJ
fullText:
Tommy's Tavern + Tap is coming to Bergen County this month as the popular pub chain is set to open in Edgewater on June 16.

Tommy's, which describes itself as a combination restaurant, bar and pizzeria, announced the opening on its Instagram page. The company has nine other locations in New Jersey, but this will be its first in New Jersey's largest county. Tommy's also has locations in Delaware and on Staten Island, New York.

Its Edgewater outpost will be at 225 River Road in the City Place Promenade shopping center. The opening has been years in the making, going back to a planning board process that started in December 2021. The eatery occupies what used to be a Pier 1 Imports store.

Owner Tommy Bonfiglio also operates the Tio Taco + Tequila Bar chain. While other restaurants struggled through the COVID pandemic, his business was able to expand, growing from three locations to 10. His Clifton spot opened in the winter of 2020.

The Tommy's menu includes classic American dishes such as burgers, pizzas, pasta, ribs, wings, salads and various other bites and sides. Tommy's also features daily drink specials with their wine, sangria, tap beer and specialty drinks. The tavern also hosts private events at select locations.

The results are in: See the Best of Bergen Food and Drink winners for 2024

The Edgewater location does not have their own website yet, but customers can get a sneak peak of what is to come at the chain's other locations.

Tommy's Tavern will join other shops and restaurants at the City Place Promenade, including Fleming's steakhouse, Greek Taverna, The Original Pancake House, Chipotle, Panera Bread and Haagen-Dazs.

title: Watch the Macy's July 4th fireworks from one of these NJ restaurants
fullText:
It's finally New Jersey's time to shine.

As you've more than likely heard by now, the annual Macy's Fourth of July fireworks show will be returning to the Hudson River for the first time in more than a decade. That means that all of North Jersey's spectacular waterfront areas in Weehawken, Hoboken and Jersey City will finally become some of the best seats in the house to view the show.

It's also the perfect opportunity to make a reservation at one of the hottest restaurants along the Hudson River to enjoy a delicious meal or handcrafted cocktail as the fireworks light up the night sky. So beat the rush and make a reservation now to guarantee yourself an unforgettable Fourth of July experience.

Chart House, Weehawken

With 24 waterfront locations across the country, Chart House was founded in 1961 by a Hawaiian surfer and a Navy man with the goal of offering fresh seafood and great views. One of its locations sits along the Hudson River in Weehawken, and is famous for its stunning panoramic views of the New York City skyline.

The menu features favorite seafood dishes like shrimp cocktail, crab cakes and coconut shrimp, as well as farm fresh fish like halibut, salmon and sea bass. There are also menu items for those not interested in seafood, including filet mignon, New York strip and herb roasted chicken. Plus, there is a 3-course meal special daily for $58, which includes a soup or salad, a choice of three entrees and a mini lava cake for dessert. To go along with the meal, Chart House has an extensive list of cocktails, wine and beer to choose from.

Hours: 4:30 to 10 p.m. Monday through Thursday; 4:30 to 10:30 p.m. Friday; 11:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. on Saturday; and 11:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. on Sunday.

Go: 1700 Harbor Blvd., Weehawken; 201-348-6628, chart-house.com/location/chart-house-weehawken-nj.

Blu on the Hudson, Weehawken

Known for its scenic view of Manhattan and modern American eats, Blu on the Hudson is a beloved spot for both holiday meals and year-round experiences. Their dinner menu includes sushi, a raw bar, homemade pasta, steak and more. The restaurant also has an extensive list of signature cocktails to enjoy while you watch the fireworks light up the Hudson River.

Hours: 4 to 10 p.m. Monday through Thursday; 4 to 11 p.m. Friday; 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. Saturday; and 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Sunday.

Go: 1200 Harbor Blvd., Weehawken; 201-636-1200, bluonthehudson.com.

NoHu Rooftop Bar & Restaurant, Weehawken

Located on top of the Envue Hotel in Weehawken, NoHu Rooftop Bar & Restaurant overlooks the Hudson River and has a breathtaking view of the New York City skyline. Because of its elevated position, it's the perfect spot for a special view of the annual Macy's Fourth of July fireworks show.

Among the items on the dinner menu include warm buttermilk biscuits, charred Brussels sprouts poutine, blackened Gulf shrimp and fried chicken strips. There is a list of cocktails, beer and wine available to accompany the meal, and their dessert menu features ice cream from Fredon Township's Windy Brow Farms.

Hours: 5 p.m. to midnight Monday through Thursday; 3 p.m. to 1:30 a.m. Friday; 11 a.m. to 1:30 a.m. Saturday; and 11 a.m. to midnight Sunday.

Go: 550 Ave. at Port Imperial, Weehawken; 201-683-2132, nohurooftopbar.com.

Halifax, Hoboken

Run by Chef Seadon Shouse and his team, Halifax in Hoboken specializes in Northeastern farm and coastal cuisine, focusing on local and sustainable ingredients from Delaware to their namesake of Halifax — the capital of Nova Scotia. Between the choice ingredients and the prime location along Hoboken's Hudson River waterfront, it's an ideal destination to enjoy a meal while watching the fireworks show.

On their dinner menu, you can expect a seafood tower, pan-seared salmon, ricotta gnocchi, prime New York strip and smoked Amish chicken. There is also an extensive dessert menu, a long list of both white and red wine, as well as speciality cocktails.

Hours: 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. Monday through Friday; and 7:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. Saturday and Sunday.

Go: 225 River St., Hoboken; 201-253-2500, halifaxhoboken.com.

Blue Eyes, Hoboken

Located in Hoboken's Frank Sinatra Park, Blue Eyes is, naturally, an Italian restaurant. In the summer months, this walk-in only restaurant has outdoor seating available so patrons can take in the stunning waterfront views.

One of the restaurant's staples is the pizza, which is authentically made using a wood-fired brick oven from Naples, Italy. Plus, the menu has an assortment of pasta dishes, appetizers, paninis, desserts, gelati and coffees available. Also in the summer months, Blue Eyes has a separate gelato stand and raw bar outside.

Hours: Noon to 10 p.m. Sunday through Thursday; and noon to 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday.

Go: 525 Sinatra Drive, Hoboken; 201-683-6861, blueeyesrestaurant.com.

Del Frisco's Grille, Hoboken

Del Frisco's Grille is a classic American chophouse chain with a trendy interior, but this location along the Hudson River in Hoboken has the added benefit of waterfront views. Menu items here include cheesesteak eggrolls, braised short rib, mahi mahi, rigatoni Bolognese, black angus streak frites and handheld burgers and sandwiches, as well as a signature steak list. You can finish off your meal with a selection from the dessert menu, or trying out one of their specialty cocktails.

Hours: 11:30 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday through Wednesday; 10:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. Thursday through Saturday; and noon to 9 p.m. on Sunday.

Go: 221 River St., Hoboken; 201-653-0195, delfriscosgrille.com/location/del-friscos-grille-hoboken-nj.

Battello, Jersey City

Yet another restaurant with stunning views of the Hudson River is Battello, a modern Italian joint with a menu that is overseen by chef and co-owner Ryan DePersio, who is also the executive chef of The Kitchen Step in Jersey City.

Though small and simple, the dinner menu is mighty. Offerings here include a seafood tower, prime filet beef carpaccio, squid ink campanelle, sheep's milk cappelletti, lasagna bianca and more. There is also a list of specialty cocktails, wines and freshly made desserts.

Hours: Open for dinner 5 to 10 p.m. Monday through Thursday; 5 to 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday; and 5 to 9 p.m. on Sunday.

Go: 502 Washington Blvd., Jersey City; 201-798-1798, battellojc.com.

Rooftop at Exchange Place, Jersey City

The Rooftop at Exchange Place offers some of the best views of the New York City skyline in New Jersey, spanning from midtown Manhattan to the city's financial district. The venue's retractable glass roof and walls make sure you don't miss any part of the view, especially during the Macy's Fourth of July fireworks show.

As for the menu, the restaurant specializes in small bites like garlic parmesan fries, mac and cheese, lollipop wings and charred broccolini caesar. But there are also more filling options, like their flat iron steak sandwich and pan-seared Atlantic salmon, available, too.

If you're not in the mood for food, order one of the bar's signature cocktails or something from their wine and beer menu.

Hours: 4 to 11 p.m. Sunday through Thursday; and 4 p.m. to 2 a.m. Friday and Saturday.

Go: 1 Exchange Place, Jersey City; 551-256-7850, rooftopxp.com.

title: Celebrity Chefs & Friends Golf and Tennis Tournament: Why to go
fullText:
"It's a golf tournament," Herb Karlitz, owner of Karlitz & Co. events marketing company, said. "But it's not really a golf tournament."

I looked around at the rolling hills of Bergen County's most picturesque country club, which, for the day, was adorned with linen-topped tables, pop-up bars and big green smokers.

"It's kind of like day camp for chefs."

Meeting each other for the first time, he welcomed me to his annual Celebrity Chefs & Friends Golf and Tennis Tournament.

According to our former food editor Esther Davidowitz: "A food festival that just happens to take place on a golf course."

And, according to me? Bergen County's culinary event of the year.

Arriving at a Bergen's most lavish food festival

My attention was originally drawn to Karlitz' Celebrity Chefs Golf Tournament by an email that described the event as a charity endeavor featuring 60(+) of the NYC-metro area's most talented chefs.

To be held at the Alpine Country Club, the day would begin with a few rounds of golf and tennis, followed by a lavish reception of decadent eats and stunning drinks. At the end of the evening, all proceeds would be donated to City Harvest, New York's largest food rescue organization.

Intrigued by the prospect of great eats for an equivalently great cause, I added my name to the guest list.

"We've got Josh Capon making lamb chops back there," Karlitz said, walking me around the club's patio, "And Marc Murphy's here with the pesto."

He motioned to the right, where Murphy, a Food Network star, stood with a pan of fresh cavatelli. He lifted pasta scoops into little wooden bowls — the aforementioned sauce dripping slowly down the sides of the serving spoon.

I vowed I would be back.

A walk amongst culinary stars

"This is amazing," I said, passing the table where Daniel Boulud's sous chef was preparing a geometrically flawless pâté en croûte. "I've never seen so much caviar and foie gras in the same place."

"It really is," Karlitz responded, "But what's even more amazing is that every one of these chefs is donating their time. They're donating their products, they're donating their evening — everything is benefitting City Harvest. It really is all about the charity."

And the guests? Paid $1,000 to $15,000 (depending on how many, if any, golfers their party would be bringing) to do the same.

We were just about done with our tour when Karlitz was distracted by golf legend, Lee Trevino. Excusing himself, the businessman urged me to enjoy my evening, promising we'd catch up later.

Considering he knew "every chef in Manhattan," and I was a fan of, well, all of them, I promised to hold him to that.

I didn't mind, though, the chance to explore the space on my own — and start trying those bougie bites.

Sampling sashimi, oxtail and more

After Karlitz left, I headed to the pool deck with my friend Ryan. About 15 food stations were set up in the area, ran by the chefs of Tatiana, Melba's and more. We started at the far corner of the space — where San Pellegrino was sponsoring the event with its crisp, cool lemonade — and worked our way around.

The first dish of the evening we tried was a live scallop crudo, prepared by chef Andy Kitko of Oceans New York. Following that, we sampled bite-sized oxtail tacos from Melba's, and fluke tostadas from Brooklyn's Ensenada. I remarked on the impressive flavor of the latter, while Ryan stopped at the bar for a drink.

"The sauce on the scallop was really creamy," he said, "Like, totally banging."

He knows what he likes.

We finished the section with some burnt end "candy" from Butcher Bar and papaya piri piri from Tatiana (prepared by sous chef Sam Zitro, because Kwame was somewhere playing golf) before heading to the main patio.

The main promenade

The set up on the patio was about triple the size of the pool deck, maybe more, with chefs just as prominent as the Top Chef champions and James Beard winners we'd just passed.

Karlitz traversed the space, eager to introduce me to Josh Beckerman, "The Foodie Magician." He was quickly distracted again by another pro athlete, though (this time, a tennis star), and was off.

As somewhat of a decorated athlete myself, however, I understood his excitement.

"This place is crawling with celebrities," Ryan said, grabbing another drink.

Whether they were truly there for the charity — or to party and flex their assets with those they assumed were on the same plane — I couldn't tell.

But, when a Goldman Sachs higher-up passed between Ryan and the bar, it was obvious the place was a hotbed for networking.

And we thought that was pretty cool.

The best dish of the night

Ryan and I were working our way through the patio (trying grand cru galbi ssam from Michelin-starred COTE and king crab rolls by chef Marcus Ware on our journey) when we saw it: the top dish of the night.

Approaching the table, which belonged to The Restaurant at Kanopi, a chef described the appetizer as the restaurant's play on beef tartare.

Featuring dry-aged meat, house-made hollandaise and some sort of rich espuma inside a crispy round shell — that resembled a golf ball itself — the amuse-bouche was a salty, fatty, melt-in-your-mouth showstopper.

I grabbed a plate of four more; originally determined to guard them with my life, but eventually swayed to share them with the biggest names in attendance (because, of course, they ran out).

It's important to note, though, that the poppers only won the night by a margin — because every complexly-flavored hors d'oeuvre was that good.

North Jersey's must-attend culinary event of the year

The sun went down late on the night of the tournament. Slowing removing its soft light from the club's manicured lawns, it took the guests with it.

By 9:15 p.m., Karlitz and I — apart from a few distant chefs — stood alone.

"This isn't real life," he said, scanning the serene landscape as the maintenance staff carried away tables. "Real life is what City Harvest deals with. Real life is 40% of people struggling with food insecurity."

"But that's why this event is so important," I responded.

Karlitz nodded. "Exactly. Because, if I can put this on for one night, 944,000 people can also eat for a night."

And it's that reality — more important than the thin-sliced truffle, peach-infused bourbon and celebrity elbow brushes — that affirmed my stated thesis: The tournament is, and in the future will persist to be, North Jersey's must-attend gastronomic evening of the year.

Kara VanDooijeweert is a food writer for NorthJersey.com and The Record. If you can't find her in Jersey's best restaurants, she's probably off running a race course in the mountains. Catch her on Instagram: @karanicolev & @northjerseyeats, and sign up for her North Jersey Eats newsletter.

title: Things to do in NJ this weekend: State Fair, concerts and more
fullText:
It's officially the first weekend of summer, so what will you be doing in North Jersey? Here are some options we've curated for you:

Summertime is the time for fairs and there's none bigger than State Fair Meadowlands, which starts on Thursday. Another way to celebrate the arrival of the season is with a summer solstice campfire and hike at Tenafly Nature Center.

There is always plenty of music in North Jersey, and this week's concerts include tributes to the Grateful Dead and Elvis Presley. There is also a cabaret show by Alan Cumming and a dance performance by Aatma Performing Arts.

We've also got sports, with Jackals baseball and the New York/New Jersey Gotham Football Club both at home this weekend; and art, with a local artist exhibit in Clifton.

And, for girls planning their quinceañera, there's a free expo this weekend.

Plus, it's Pride Month, so check out our big list of Pride events, some of which are also included below.

Enjoy!

Sunny and hot, with only a small chance of showers

According to the National Weather Service:

  • Thursday night: Partly cloudy, with a low around 75.
  • Friday: Mostly sunny with a high at almost 100, with mostly cloudy skies at night and a low in the mid-70s.
  • Saturday: Partly sunny, with a high in the mid-90s and chance of showers. Mostly cloudy at night and more possible showers, with a low in the mid-70s
  • Sunday: Partly sunny, with a high in the low 90s and a chance of showers.

'Artists’ Perspectives' at Clifton Arts Center

Through June 29, the “Artists’ Perspectives” exhibition by the Community Arts Association will be on display at the Clifton Arts Center. The exhibit is about how artists use perspective techniques to create realistic and non-realistic impressions. The artist’s perspective values process, communication and understanding. It embraces emotion and encourages connection. When artists communicate information, in this case through paintings, their perspectives can help make that visual information accessible, comprehensible and approachable. The artist’s perspective can also shape how we think about and act with each other as a community at large.

The Community Arts Association originated in Allendale in 1965. Meetings were originally held in the Highlands Presbyterian Church before relocating to Northern Highlands Regional School, Archer United Methodist Church and finally to Trinity Episcopal Church. Community Arts Association sponsors workshops, hosts demonstrations, lectures, day trips, and art scholarships for graduating high schoolers.

Go: "Artists' Perspectives" by the Community Arts Association at Clifton Arts Center, 900 Clifton Ave. $3 admission. Normal gallery hours are Wednesday through Saturday, 1 to 4 p.m. 973-472-5499. cliftonartscenter.org

State Fair Meadowlands at MetLife Stadium

The fair is back with a lineup of new and favorite all-ages entertainment. This year’s program is packed with stunts and acrobatic acts, amusement rides, magicians, musicians, racing pigs and food. For the next 17 days, the fair will be open in the stadium's parking lots E and F, on weeknights (except June 25) and with extended hours on weekends and July 4. Parking is free in lots G, J and L for all fairgoers.

Go: State Fair Meadowlands at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford. Thursday, Monday and Wednesday, 6 p.m. to midnight; Friday, 6 p.m. to 1 a.m.; Saturday, 2 p.m. to 1 a.m.; Sunday, 2 p.m. to midnight. metlifestadium.com.

Grateful Dead tribute in Millburn

The music of the Grateful Dead continues to grow and evolve, long after the band played their last show. The members of Workingman's Jed share a common love for the Dead’s musical canon, jams and multi-part vocal harmonies. They strive to honor the original compositions through their individual styles and musical experiences, to create something familiar, yet different and special. They design unique set lists for each show, merge songs together in original ways, and try to do new things. ​

Go: Workingman's Jed at Taylor Park, 110 Main St., Millburn. 7 to 8:30 p.m. Thursday (rain date is June 27). Free. twp.millburn.nj.us

Jackals baseball at Hinchliffe Stadium

The Jackals are home in Paterson this weekend, with a three-game series against the Quebec Capitales.

Friday is '70s Night, so dress up in your best '70s outfit. On Saturday, there will be a mini-bat giveaway and a post-game firework show. Sunday is Family Day with $5 tickets for kids age 12 and under and seniors age 55 and over.

Go: New Jersey Jackals at Hinchliffe Stadium, 1 Jasper St., Paterson. 6:35 p.m. Friday, 6:05 p.m. Saturday, 4:35 p.m. Sunday, $5 to $25. jackals.com, 973-746-7434, contact@jackals.com. Gates open an hour prior to the start of the game.

'Big Gay Cabaret' in Fair Lawn

Celebrate Pride Month at this fundraiser for the Old Library Theatre and the Bergen County LGBTQ+ Alliance, Friday and Saturday at the George Frey Performing Arts Center. The show is co-directed by Jeff Parsons and Dave Toussas, with musical direction by Christopher Vehmas.

Go: "Big Gay Cabaret" at the George Frey Performing Arts Center, 10-10 20th St., Fair Lawn. 7:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday. $25. oldlibrarytheatre.com.

'Sounds of My Soul' dance showcase at NJPAC

Aatma Performing Arts celebrates its 15-year anniversary with “Sounds of My Soul” on Saturday. Directed by Amit Shah, the show features hits from Bollywood films and an eclectic fusion of Indian folk and western pop music. Highlights include handmade costumes and excerpts from Aatma’s newest touring production, “Finding Home: An Indian Musical.”

Go: Aatma Performing Arts presents "Sounds of My Soul" at NJPAC, Prudential Hall, Betty Wold Johnson Stage. 6 p.m. Saturday. $59 to $149. njpac.org.

The David Drumgold Variety Show – Pride Edition

Actor and Broadway/TV/film producer David Drumgold brings a special Pride edition of his variety show to the Puffin Cultural Forum in Teaneck on Saturday. Hearkening back to the variety shows of the '60s and '70s - like "The Carol Burnett Show," "The Flip Wilson Show," and "The Cher Show" - Drumgold's variety show features good old-fashioned talent, cheer and the escapism of a good time. It celebrates everything magical about art, and features comedy, drag, dance and musicians.

Featured performers include the New York Metropolitan Opera soprano Brandie Inez Sutton, pianist Yasuhiko Fukuoka, and R&B/soul singer Diana Taylor. Plus, the newest addition to the lineup is Pissi Myles, a drag comedian, singer and hostess.

N95 or equivalent masks are required. A limited quantity will be available at the door.

Go: "The David Drumgold Variety Show – Pride Edition" at the Puffin Cultural Forum, 20 Puffin Way, Teaneck. 7 p.m. Saturday. $10 suggested donation. RSVP at daviddrumgoldprideatpuffin.eventbrite.com or call 201-836-3499. Those who cannot pay the suggested donation may call (or write to aortega@puffinfoundation.org) to make free reservations.

Alan Cumming at State Theatre

"Alan Cumming: Uncut - With Henry Koperski at the Piano" - Cumming's new cabaret show - comes to State Theatre New Jersey in New Brunswick on Saturday.

A longtime TV, film and stage actor, Cumming premiered his first cabaret show, "Alan Cumming Sings Sappy Songs," in 2015 in New York City. His next cabaret show, "Legal Immigrant," debuted in 2018, followed by "Alan Cumming Is Not Acting His Age," which toured the world and ended up on Broadway. He is currently touring with NPR’s Ari Shapiro in "Och and Oy: A Considered Cabaret!," as well as "Uncut," which he developed at the Yaddo artists retreat and premiered in April.

This show is recommended for ages 18 and up. Everyone, regardless of age, entering the theater must purchase a ticket.

Go: "Alan Cumming: Uncut" at State Theatre of New Jersey, 15 Livingston Ave., New Brunswick. 8 p.m. Saturday. $39 to $69. stnj.org, 732-246-7469.

NY/NJ Gotham soccer in Harrison Sunday

Sunday is Kids Day at the Red Bull Arena, with a Fan Fest before the New York/New Jersey Gotham Football Club takes on the Washington Spirit in women's pro soccer action. The Fan Fest will feature an Eli Manning meet-and-greet, balloon artists, face paint, friendship bracelet-making and food trucks.

Go: NY/NJ Gotham FC with Fan Fest at Red Bull Arena, 600 Cape May St., Harrison. Sunday. Fan Fest at 11 a.m. Game at 1:30 p.m. $15 to $270.21. gothamfc.com.

Quinceañera Expo in Saddle Brook

Young ladies and their parents planning their quinceañera celebrations can attend NJ Quinceañera Expo 2024 in Saddle Brook on Sunday. The expo will feature an array of vendors and exhibitors showcasing the latest trends in quinceañera dresses, decorations, photography, catering, entertainment and more. Attendees will have the opportunity to connect with industry professionals, discover unique ideas and find everything needed to create a memorable quinceañera.

Highlights of the expo include a fashion show with the latest gown designs on the runway, vendor booths, exclusive offers, raffles and prizes, and expert advice to help make your quinceañera dream a reality.

Go: NJ Quinceañera Expo 2024 at Crowne Plaza, 50 Kenny Place, Saddle Brook. 2 to 7 p.m. Sunday. Free admission. For information, call 862-600-1769.

Summer Solstice campfire and night hike

Celebrate the longest day of the year and the official start of the summer with the Tenafly Nature Center. A TNC naturalist will lead participants on a night hike to experience the sounds of summer, followed by a campfire and s'mores. The program is intended for adults and families with children 5 and up. Children must be accompanied by an adult. The program will be held entirely outdoors. In case of inclement weather, it will be held under cover. Social distancing in effect. Space is limited and advance registration is required.

Go: Summer Family Hike at the Tenafly Nature Center, 313 Hudson Ave., Tenafly. 7 to 9 p.m. Sunday. $8 for members; $12 for non-members; free for children under age 2. tenaflynaturecenter.org, 201-568-6093.

Jesse Garron's Tribute To Elvis

Billed as "The Closest Thing to the King," Garron uses the name of Elvis Presley's twin brother who died at birth as he pays tribute to Elvis and his legacy. Inspired by Elvis at the age of four, Garron was always mesmerized by Elvis' voice and intrigued by everything Elvis from his music to his movies. He got his first break to pay him tribute at the age of 17 in a high school talent show and won the popular vote. Since his first performance in 1997, he has performed around the country and the world. In 2019, he was inducted into the International Elvis Tribute Artist Hall of Fame for his dedication to keeping Elvis' legacy alive. Garron performs with a four-piece band and three backing vocalists.

Go: Jesse Garron's Tribute to Elvis at the Florham Park gazebo, 111 Ridgedale Ave., on the Great Lawn, at 7 p.m. Sunday. If weather is questionable, visit florhamparkgazebo.com for updates. Free.

Have an event coming up? Tell us about it. Write to Daniel Galioto at galiotod@northjersey.com.

title: NJ teen creates music program to help non-white classical students
fullText:
There's a moment of truth, for every young musician.

Between the time they first touch a violin, at perhaps age 5, and the time they make their debut at Carnegie Hall, there's a moment when they're tempted to quit.

True, for every kid. And truer still for young musicians of color — who often get small encouragement from a culture that, historically, doesn't see the New York Philharmonic as a career goal for them. By the time they reach high school, many are ready to throw in the towel.

Marie Dillard, the 18-year-old creator of The Crescendo Lab, knows. She might have been one of them.

"I just felt left out," she said. "There was no reason to see myself in classical music."

That's the reason Dillard, a lifelong Englewood resident, created a program to encourage those kids to stay on track. She just received $5,000 from the Prudential Emerging Visionaries program to take her Crescendo Lab to the next level.

"It's about empowering them and inspiring them to continue to play classical music, and just stick with it," said Dillard, herself a violist.

"When I got to high school I saw so many kids, especially Black and brown kids, who played classical music in middle school, and quit before high school," she said.

Grown from seed

Last summer, using $750 in seed money she got from the Be All You entrepreneurship program, she began The Crescendo Lab with five students, ages 5 to 12, whom she mentored out of an office in Englewood. It's an offshoot of her own nonprofit Persistent Endeavors Foundation.

"It's a classical music mentoring program that focuses on Black and brown students," she said. "With a sort of historic lens. I will mentor them, and show them people who look like them. When I started playing classical music, I didn't see a lot of people who looked like me."

The five-week, once-a-week course was not just about teaching these kids to be better musicians. It's also — and crucially — about teaching them that people of color have a place in classical music.

How, after all, can you imagine doing something that you've never seen anyone else like you do?

"I'd never heard of Black people composing classical music," she said. "That was something I never really thought of. If you think of a Black composer, you think of jazz. Black people have sort of been put into this category. 'This is your music.' "

There are, of course, plenty of Black classical composers — though they tend to be overlooked in standard survey courses. Joseph Bologne, the 18th century French violinist and composer, subject of the 2022 biopic "Chevalier," is one. Dillard teaches her students about him. Florence Price, who composed over 300 works including four symphonies, is another. Then there's Scott Joplin, whose "ragtime" pieces were actually elegant concert works (he also wrote two operas).

There are plenty of others: William Grant Still, Ulysses Kay, Louis Moreau Gottschalk, James P. Johnson (he did concert works like "Yamacraw," in addition to composing jazz), Terence Blanchard, and more.

Music appreciation

Such names tend not to be so well known, by white or Black kids. "Anytime I hear of any programs that had to do with Black kids and music, it only had to do with hop-hop, something like that," she said. "That makes sense. I don't blame them for that. But at the same time, I never had anyone saying, 'Hey, I'm a Black person, I play classical music.' "

She herself was lucky: she grew up in a house where both parents had been musicians. Mom played violin. Dad played sax and piano.

"Growing up, I was exposed to all kinds of music," she said. "I started at a very young age. It wasn't until 4 that I picked up an instrument."

It was the violin: Her mother had a theory about it. Rubbing the bow on the strings with one hand, while fingering with the other, brought both sides of the brain into play. "Your brain is crossing hemispheres," Dillard said. "There's something fundamental to learning that happens to your brain."

In middle school (Elisabeth Morrow) she switched to viola, which has been her go-to instrument ever since. She recently graduated from St. Andrews, a private school in Delaware. She'll be entering the University of Pennsylvania in the fall. But wherever she goes, she'll take The Crescendo Lab with her.

"I'm thinking of a recorded series of short-form videos, where I talk about the lives of Black and brown composers," she said. "I want to grow an online curriculum. And I want to interview Black and brown musicians today, who are in this area. There's so much more to do."

title: Newark North to Shore festival: Kevin Hart among headliners
fullText:
The blues is music.

The blues is a mental condition.

The blues is music about a mental condition. Specifically, the condition of sadness. More specifically: sadness as the result of oppression, injustice and waking up this morning to find your baby gone.

So it's not so far-fetched that this summer's second annual North to Shore Festival, running through June 30, should feature among its 200 attractions a program called "Chasing the Blues Away, featuring The Blues People and NJ Mental Health Players." (June 26).

It's a collaboration between a blues band and an acting collective — one that specializes in scenarios related to mental health.

"Music in general, and particularly the blues, is about sharing life experiences," said David Rodriguez, executive producer of the festival, and himself a musician. "And sometimes those experiences are more clouds than sunshine. The sharing of pain as well as the sharing of happiness is part of the process. Highlighting that in the festival is a critical way to deal with these issues upfront."

And it's one of many examples of how the month-long, three-city, multi-venue arts festival is using the arts to address issues of wellness — both mental and physical.

"I think the whole thought of the program is to really make it a festival with a soul," Rodriguez said.

Coming to North Jersey

The North Jersey leg of the festival — centering around Newark — runs June 23 to 30. Two earlier parts of the festival are based in Asbury Park (June 10 to 16) and Atlantic City (June 17 to 23).

All of them feature an eclectic mix of entertainment: stars and unknowns, music and comedy, film and visual arts and discussion groups and tech talks.

"I think the whole thought of the program is to really make it a festival with a soul," Rodriguez said.

The Newark segment, featuring over 50 attractions, includes some big name entertainers, including Matchbox Twenty (June 27), A Day to Remember (June 26), Jeezy and Scarface (June 28), writer-director Kevin Smith (June 30), comedian Kevin Hart (June 30), and — a late breaking addendum, in association with the Montclair Film Festival — actor Paul Giamatti in conversation with Stephen Colbert (July 26).

But this year, issues of mental and physical health were never very far from the programmers' thinking.

"The cornerstone is, we're not doctors, we're not psychologists, we're not any of that," said Rodriguez, an Englewood resident. "But we can share a message for people who might otherwise not hear it. The one thing the arts can do better than anything is bring people together, and share messages that affect not only them but friends and family members."

This year's festival includes a New Davonhaime Food Bank Distribution Day, combining art and nourishment (June 24 and 25). There is a "Rest Fest" at The Newark Museum of Art (June 30).

The NJ Mental Health Players make an appearance on several other bills including The Ultimate Jazz and R&B Jam (June 25) and Jazz and Joy featuring Lynette Sheard Experience (June 28). And a virtual program on June 26 is called Prescribing Creativity: Promoting Health Equity through Arts-on-Prescription.

"Mental wellness is a great part of physical wellness," Rodriguez said. "We're working with Horizon and RWJBarnabas. Physicians can prescribe arts activities, whether it be Zumba classes or a ticket to a comedy show or tickets for family activities. The arts can be a vehicle to enhance physical wellness through mental wellness."

This is the second year of North to Shore — N2S — the Garden State's answer to South by Southwest — SXSW. Last year's inaugural festival drew 220,000 people over the month. This year, they're expecting more.

"The first year, it was all we could do to make it successful," Rodriguez said. "The second year, we're saying, how can we make what we've created impactful? And our hope is that next year, the impact becomes even greater."

title: Broadway: Home revival written by Samm-Art-Williams-died
fullText:
The first Broadway revival of Samm-Art Williams’ “Home” is full of joy and pain, heart and hope.

And sorrow, for the playwright passed away days before the first preview. But rest assured Williams is smiling from above after every performance, for this atypical work is engrossing and entertaining  

The story is about Cephus Miles (Tory Kittles), a Black farmer in North Carolina. He’s in love with Pattie Mae (Brittany Inge), who goes off to college. But things take a turn when he is thrown in jail for opposing the Vietnam War draft. And when he moves to the big city, his life becomes dangerous and complicated.

Directed by the Tony Award-winning Kenny Leon, the script in this 90-minute show is packed with poetry, melody, rhythm and song.

There's talk of land, soil, sun, rain and crops.

God, faith and family — and America.

There are dozens of characters, but only three people in this small-scale but mighty production. The acting is first-rate. Stori Ayers is identified as Woman Two in the program, but she portrays everyone from a a youngster to a prison guard to a bus driver. Watching her transform from one moment to the next is one of the highlights of the night.

The audience warms up to Kittles quickly. He allows us to share Cephus' tragedy as he goes from the comforts of home to jail to being lost among the masses, peddling for cash any way he can.

Inge plays multiple characters, too, but she shines bright as Pattie Mae. Maybe it's her eyes? Her smile? There's real chemistry between Inge and Kittles that is wonderful to see.

The minimal set by Arnulfo Maldonado works, as does lighting by Allen Lee Hughes, costumes by Dede Ayite, sound design by Justin Ellington, and hair and wig design by Nikiya Mathis. Kate Wilson deserves mention as voice coach.  

Everything comes together to make this a feel-good evening. The ending may be predictable, but that’s OK.

“Home” opens the 2024-25 season, and it’s timing could not be better. What are the tens of thousands of migrants looking for? Jobs, opportunities, a place to start again.

The work also gives voice to the poor and lonely and homeless — and anyone in America looking for a place to fit in, to belong.

And it's a reminder that no matter how far away we go, we can’t escape who we are, where we come from.

Home will always be a part of us.

Go: “Home,” through July 21, Todd Haimes Theatre, 227 W. 42nd St., New York, $49 to $149; 212-719-1300, roundabouttheatre.org.

Bill Canacci can be reached at bcanacci@gannettnj.com.

title: What are zombie mortgages? Foreclosure looms over old loans
fullText:
The term sounds like something out of a horror movie. And for many homeowners, the prospect of losing their homes due to so-called "zombie mortgages" is quite scary.

But thousands of Americans are facing that possibility today, thanks to a combination of opportunistic vendors amid a housing boom and confusion over the status of long-ago loans.

The origin of the problem dates back roughly two decades to the housing bubble of the mid-2000s. Lenders offered prospective homebuyers two mortgages in the form of 80/20 loans, with the second 20% mortgage taking the place of a down payment.

A few years later, amid the housing market crash during the 2008 financial crisis, the government began advocating for loan modifications on mortgages to curb the increase in foreclosures. For many people, that meant their 20% mortgage was forgiven — or so they thought.

Instead, the lenders frequently sold the loans to debt collectors at a fraction of the price, often without homeowners knowing. Now, the collectors are seeking payment of the zombie mortgage — a loan homebuyers thought was dead — along with interest and other fees accumulated over time.

An NPR investigation found more than 10,000 people in New York alone have received foreclosure notices over second mortgages in the past two years. The homeowners are faced with the choice of either repaying the loans, in some cases hundreds of thousands of dollars, or losing their house.

The situations has led to confusion for homeowners, who assumed — and in many cases were told explicitly by lenders — that they no longer had to repay their second mortgages after the loan modification. Some reported receiving foreclosure warnings by mail and telephone but believed them to be scams.

Fighting back

Fortunately for those at risk of losing their home, lawyers have been hard at work searching for ways to fight this relatively new real estate trend. And one legal statute cited by NPR has at least provided a temporary reprieve to the foreclosure process.

According to Virginia-based attorney Kristi Kelly, Regulation Z of the Truth in Lending Act requires companies to send monthly statements for any interest assessed on a mortgage. In most instances, Kelly said, these statements never arrived, and the collectors are now looking to retroactively tack on the interest fees.

Exploring legal options to fight zombie mortgages is one such strategy for homeowners who are unable to pay off their remaining loan or unwilling to sell the home. A CBS News story also suggests trying to negotiate a settlement, resulting in a lower, lump-sum payment than the total mortgage and interest.

title: What happens if you miss jury duty? We asked experts
fullText:
Serving on a jury can be a gratifying experience, yet so many people find ways to get out of it.

What happens when a person doesn't show up for jury duty, whether on purpose or by accident? In truth, the consequences vary depending on the judge.

Anthony Talarico, the chief assistant prosecutor for the Major Crimes Unit at the Bergen County Prosecutor's Office, said failure to respond to a jury questionnaire or summons is "in the discretion of the court."

Talarico said without a reasonable excuse, a person who fails to show up is liable for a $500 fine or could be punished for contempt of court, a fourth-degree indictable offense. Contempt of court could land someone in state prison for up to 18 months.

According to the assistant prosecutor, a judge could direct the sheriff to send the person a written notice to respond to the questionnaire and let them know a fine has been imposed on them and they have 30 days to respond to the notice. If they fail to respond, the assignment judge could have the sheriff recover the $500 from the person.

"We're not going through jury questionnaires and seeing who hasn't responded and looking to prosecute them," Talarico said. "Obviously that's ridiculous."

Talarico said the purpose of the statutes is to empower the court to fine people or threaten to fine people who don't respond, and it is just looking for people to respond to the questionnaires. It is unlikely a judge would place a person in jail for failing to show up for jury duty. The assistant prosecutor said the court doesn't want people throwing the notices away and when someone doesn't fill it out, the person is required to show up in person.

"And what this is really saying is: 'Hey, we really want you to respond to this. If you don't respond to the questionnaire, you're definitely going to have to come in and explain why," Talarico said.

He said if a reasonable excuse is given, a person can be excused from jury duty.

Talarico said jury duty is an important constitutional right and that a small number of people are ever called to serve. He said a majority of people are excused for a cause or excused because there is no trial going on.

He said the last published case he could find of someone being fined and having assets seized was in 1838 in Mercer County and the person did get his $1 fine back. However, people should still respond to jury duty summons as the 1838 case is just the last published case, and you could still be fined.

"The Founding Fathers did put it up there with the same category as representative government as how important trial by jury is," Talarico said. "John Adams said it was the hearts and lungs of liberty, trial by jury, just like representative government."

Everyone has a constitutional right to a jury trial under federal and state constitutions and Talarico said the government doesn't ask much of its citizens. He said they aren't required to vote, aren't required to serve in the military and are only asked to pay taxes and serve on a jury.

"It is baked into the fabric of who we are as Americans," Talarico said, adding it is a "cornerstone" of people's rights.

Talarico said many people who end up serving on a jury become invested in the trial, and even if it ends up being longer than anticipated, they rarely object.

Defense attorney Brian Neary said serving on a jury should be as cherished as the right to vote.

"I think there's an obligation of education," Neary said. "The system of justice has to educate people of its importance. School has to educate people of its importance."

In Bergen County, the courts are backed up because of the pandemic, and Talarico said they didn't try cases for over two years. He said they are just starting to get through the backlog.

Neary said he argued about virtual jury selection before the state Supreme Court, noting there was an issue about who would have connectivity and the potential to exclude people who could not work the technology or couldn't afford to have a device that could connect them.

"It became a big brouhaha about that where now, they're required to keep statistics about who calls up and says 'I can't come because I've got to go to Disneyland or I can't come because I've got to go to work,' " Neary said.

Neary added there is a "deeper" side to jury selection because a jury of peers is a cross-section of the community. He said it is a "tremendous amount of responsibility" to be on a jury.

"Everybody who serves on a jury thinks that it is worthwhile and important experience," Neary said. "They don't want to do it but after they finished, not only are they glad they did it, but understand how important and what a meaningful experience it is to a person."

title: Photo galleries of 2024 North Jersey proms
fullText:
June means high school senior proms in North Jersey and NorthJersey.com was all over taking photos of high schoolers dressed to the nines for their special night. Some rented snazzy cars, others took stretch limos.

The large scale venues varied, from the Old Tappan Manor and Nanina's in the Park in Belleville to The Brownstone in Paterson and the Rockleigh and Westmount country clubs. title: First ever Splash 'n Dash set at River Edge Swim Club in NJ
fullText:
Bergen County residents have a new opportunity to engage in friendly competition, where swimmers need to put their running shoes on — and runners need to bring a bathing suit.

The River Edge Swim Club holds its first-ever Splash N’ Dash Biathlon on Saturday, June 22. All Bergen County residents are welcome to compete in the event. 

Contestants will swim laps in the 25-meter-laned pool, then run on the swim club grounds and nearby athletic field.

Story continues below photo gallery

There are 14 events, and ages range from 5 to 18 and over. The number of pool laps and running distance is based on the seven different age brackets. For each age group, there is a male and female race. 

The event is open to all residents because the club wanted to “engage in real friendly county competition,” said Christopher McGee, a member of the River Edge Swim Club board of trustees. Local swim clubs, gyms, and high school swim teams were invited to broaden the reach of the event. 

McGee says the race gives competitors who are solely runners or swimmers a chance to try something different and get out of their comfort zone, as well as a fun opportunity for kids to compete against each other.

“When I was little, everyone was swimming. Swimming is something kids don’t normally do anymore,” said River Edge swim coach Ryan Berman. “It is a great way to get kids involved that they may not ever compete in."

Berman is the head coach of the 11 and up swim team and wants her team to try hard, but especially have fun. 

Swim clubs dwindling

The club hopes the event encourages kids to spend more time outside — and swimming. “Any way of getting kids out and moving is a good idea, go out and go for a swim, do a little exercise,” said Teresa Donohue, head of the aquatics program and club president. 

COVID-19 hurt the club's participation the past few years, but the biathlon offers a chance to start fresh. “Things have been different since COVID," said McGee. "Getting the kids back together and thinking of new ways to get everyone at the pool is amazing.”  

McGee said swim clubs are dwindling, due to closures spurred by financial issues. McGee said the event can show residents that “we have a great swim club in the county.”

“Swim clubs have been the life and blood of summertime in Bergen County,” he said.

Donohue agreed. “We hope that people coming and seeing what we have to offer will get us new members,” she said. “We just want people to have a good time. It accomplishes some good will between towns, and people that don’t know each other will chat while waiting for their turn to swim.”

title: Police officers with religious garb, beards find protections in law
fullText:
In police departments across the region, more police officers are sporting beards or religious garb such as hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.

It was not always that way.

In a lawsuit 25 years ago, two Muslim officers sued the Newark Police Department after they faced disciplinary charges over beards that they wore for religious reasons. They argued in the Third Circuit Court of Appeals that a policy requiring officers to be clean shaven, allowing only for medical exceptions, violated their religious freedoms.

Justice Samuel Alito’s opinion, filed March 3, 1999, stated the police department did not give “substantial justification for refusing to provide similar treatment for officers who are required to wear beards for religious reasons.” Alito, now a U.S. Supreme Court Justice, concluded that the policy violated their First Amendment rights.

Shakoor Mustafa, one of the two Muslim officers who sued the department, recalled that the courtroom erupted in cries of Allahu-Akbar, meaning God is greatest, when the decision was announced.

“Everyone was ecstatic,” said Mustafa, a devout Muslim who continues to wear a beard. “We came out of courtroom, and I had tears in my eyes.”

“It's significant to recognize people's religious rights,” Mustafa added. “This is what the whole case was about. It was about the religious rights and the freedom of people — me just trying to gain my right as a citizen who was a police officer.”

In recent years, New Jersey law enforcement agencies have faced a growing number of requests for religious exceptions to uniform and grooming policies as the population, and its police, have grown more diverse. While federal and state laws protect employees seeking religious accommodations, some conflicts have arisen over such requests.

Legal protections for religious rights

Under New Jersey anti-discrimination law, an employer may be required to permit employees to wear attire or maintain facial hair required by their religious beliefs "as long as it does not impose an undue hardship on the employer’s business."

Title VII of the federal Civil Rights Act of 1964 also requires that employers make exceptions to their rules or preferences to allow employees to follow religious dress and grooming practices.

Lori Windham, vice president and senior counsel at the Beckett Fund, a nonprofit legal institute focused on religious freedom, said the law was clear: if you make beard exceptions for medical reasons, you have to make them for religious reasons too.

Beckett represented Shakoor and fellow officer, the late Faruq Abdul-Aziz, 25 years ago, but most cases since then have involved the military and not police departments, Windham said.

“We had Navy, Army and Marine cases involving service members wanting to wear beards while serving their country,” Windham said. “Those cases have been successful.”

“The law has strong protections for police officers to be able to follow their faith,” Windham added.

The International Association of Chiefs of Police Policy Center also recommends in its guidance that departments make exceptions for religious reasons and for medical reasons. The medical exemption typically involves Black officers affected with pseudofolliculitis barbae, a skin condition that makes shaving painful.

Calls for a state directive

Lt. Kamil Warriach, president of the New Jersey-based Muslim American Law Enforcement Association, said that while officers have had requests for beards or religious head dress granted, it has not always been easy. Some officers and academy cadets have faced delays or pushback, he said.

“People have gotten slack for it,” he said. “They don’t want to push the issue because people take it personally and executives may retaliate against you."

In Perth Amboy, a traffic officer sued the police department in March alleging religious discrimination. Among the reasons, he said he faced unreasonable obstacles when he requested to grow a beard, which he said was part of his faith tradition as a Coptic Orthodox Christian. His request was not approved for about a year despite obtaining a letter from a priest and verbal pleas to command staff, while two other officers got approval for similar requests within a week, the lawsuit stated.

In Jersey City, an officer sued in 2021 over alleged harassment and retaliation linked to a religious exemption to the dress code. He got an exemption to wear a beard, but a supervisor reprimanded him for a beard that was deemed too manicured.

In at least two cases in New Jersey, Warraich said women were “given a hard time” when they asked to wear a hijab in training or on the job as police officers. He called for the state to issue guidance or a directive for police department on religious exceptions to dress codes.

“It’s a problem because it’s left up to the discretion of the people in charge,” Warraich said. “A solution is a directive which would just tell anyone that any religious article, like a yarmulke or a turban for a Sikh male or a head covering for a Muslim or Sikh female, any religious item, should be allowed.”

Dan Prochilo, a spokesman for the New Jersey Attorney General's Office, said that "policies governing law enforcement officers’ appearance, including rules surrounding facial hair and attire worn while on duty, are within the purview of individual departments and law enforcement executives."

Some departments are clarifying their policies to meet the demands of an increasingly diverse police force. For instance, Newark announced in 2021 that, per official policy, it would allow women in the police force the option to wear hijab.

The New York Police Department relaxed its facial hair rules in 2020, two years after a settlement was made in a class-action lawsuit filed by a Muslim cop over the no-beard policy. They initially allowed beards for all officers, but in May, the NYPD reversed that policy, once again banning beards except for religious or medical exemptions.

In the NYPD case and the Newark case 25 years ago, police officials said beards had posed a safely risk with the wearing of safety equipment such as a gas masks or N95 masks. Attorneys argued that exceptions already exits for medical reasons and for undercover officers.

Asked about safety concerns, Warraich said police officers did not carry masks and it was rare to wear them, or "almost non-existent."

A state policy would signal that diversity is welcome

Police agencies would benefit from a state policy clarifying rules on beards and religious garb because it would signal to diverse groups that they are welcome in the ranks. In the police academy, a written directive would help because some lack confidence to ask for waivers at the start of their training, Warrraich said.

“I talk to a lot of young people and, believe it or not, it’s a big deal to them,” Warraich said. “They don’t want to cut off their beard in the policy academy.”

Mustafa reflected on his case 25 years ago. He said he felt “naked” when he shaved the beard that he wore in accordance with his Muslim faith entering the police academy. He grew it back later when he went undercover busting drug deals in Newark.

He had worn it for years on the job when, suddenly, the chief of police decided to enforce a 1971 order banning beards. He believed it was an act of retaliation by the mayor. He had previously served on the mayor's security team and said they had a disagreement.

Mustafa knows that the 1999 ruling in Fraternal Order of Police v. City of Newark has been cited in other cases and was covered by many media outlets. For him, the goal of his lawsuit was not to best the police department, but to be true to his faith.

After he won his case, an Orthodox Jewish man from New York City sought him out for guidance in a religious discrimination case against the NYPD. A Christian woman also cited his case when she argued she should not be compelled to work on Sundays.

“I’m not interested in being a crusader,” Mustafa said, “but I will always help anyone I can. It’s the nature of being a servant of God. I will come anywhere to stand with people, to stand with this issue.”
seoTitle: Police officers with religious garb, beards find protections in law

title: Bergenfield NJ school employee files retaliation lawsuit
fullText:
A Bergenfield school district employee said she is owed back wages and was unfairly retaliated against after she filed gender discrimination complaints against other administrators.

Ligia Alberto said she worked as a school counselor from 2010 to 2015, as the director of testing, teaching and learning from 2015 to 2018 and has been the director of the alternative school, testing and data analysis since 2018.

In a lawsuit filed against the district in Bergen County Superior Court, Alberto said she was subjected to "gender discriminatory comments," shown less favor than male colleagues and nothing was done by the administration when she brought these issues up.

Superintendent Christopher Tully, Bergenfield High School Principal Jim Fasano and the board of education are all named in the lawsuit in addition to the district. Tully said the district does not comment on personnel and litigation.

According to the lawsuit, Alberto "performed her duties in an exemplary fashion" and had positive performance reviews which led to her promotion as the director of the district's alternative school. The suit said the school was "severely mismanaged, disorganized and failing to provide an appropriate education for students" before she took over and revamped it.

Alberto said Fasano continually referred to her as "young woman" even though she asked him to refer to her as Dr. Alberto. She said she complained to Darlene Markman, the assistant superintendent, and Tully about Fasano's comments and no action was taken. The lawsuit said Fasano would refer to Alberto's male colleagues by their name and not "young man" and he would show them favoritism.

NJ news George Norcross III, South Jersey’s Democratic power broker, faces racketeering charges

On June 16, 2022, Alberto filed an affirmative action complaint, alleging gender discrimination and she said it resulted in Fasano retaliating against her by ignoring her and "treating her like a pariah."

In July 2022, Alberto requested to go on a sabbatical leave which was part of the collective bargaining agreement.

Alberto said her sabbatical aligned with district goals and told Tully she would be teaching and conducting research at Felician University in Rutherford during her leave. The lawsuit said Alberto agreed to delay her sabbatical until January 2023 to find a replacement for her.

According to the lawsuit, district policy would pay half of an administrator's salary for one year and administrators are not required to perform work for the district or school board while on sabbatical.

Alberto said in September 2022, Tully called her into his office to tell her the board had approved her sabbatical from January 2023 until January 2024 and gave her a sidebar agreement document that he said had to be signed for her to go on leave. The agreement document had a provision that required Alberto to continue her duties as the district's testing coordinator and work with the assistant superintendent for curriculum and instruction while on leave.

The suit accuses Tully of "falsely representing" that Alberto had to sign the agreement to go on sabbatical, which she did under "false representations." She said she signed the agreement believing she would be "fully compensated" for working as the district testing coordinator and for working with the assistant superintendent for curriculum and instruction.

According to the lawsuit, Alberto was "purposefully singled out" because she was a woman and she filed the discrimination complaint against Fasano and Tully. She said she wasn't compensated fully for continuing to work despite being on sabbatical and was required to attend the district's administrative retreat in August 2023 but was not compensated.

Alberto said she complained to Tully that she should be compensated for continuing to work with the district while out on sabbatical. The lawsuit said in October 2023, Tully "threatened" Alberto if she didn't continue to do her job as as the district testing coordinator and the collaborative work while on leave and without additional compensation, she would be fired. According to the lawsuit, the sidebar agreement ended in June 2023.

Alberto filed a second discrimination charge in October 2023 which she said resulted in more retaliatory actions including being told by Tully in November 2023 that the district would no longer pay her any money for the remainder of her sabbatical and she would be placed on leave without pay because of the discrimination charge. The lawsuit said Alberto was further threatened by Tully that "her conduct" would be considered as a part of her annual evaluation for 2023-2024.

The suit said no actions were taken and nothing was investigated despite Alberto's complaints. She said the district continued to single her out, failing to pay her for going to the Middle States Annual Commissioner's Meeting in Philadephia, leaving her out of the district's annual Christmas celebration and failing to pay her and credit her vacation days. The lawsuit stated Alberto was owed $100,000 and she was dropped from the pension system for a year, which made her lose benefits.

According to the lawsuit, Alberto is still entitled to a one-year sabbatical since she worked for 10 months and the district created a hostile work environment and caused her "severe emotional distress." The suit said the stress from the situation has caused "uncontrollable eye twitching and bouts of severe emotional trauma and anxiety." She sought a medical leave of absence from Jan. 15 until Feb. 26 because of panic attacks caused by what happened.

title: Sheraton Crossroads site: Mahwah NJ Planning Board decides future
fullText:
MAHWAH — A proposal to include data and fulfillment centers as possible uses on the Sheraton Crossroads site is "not inconsistent" with the township's master plan, its Planning Board ruled Monday.

It is the first action taken about the site since the hotel closed in December.

The developer, Crossroads Hotel Developers LLC, originally proposed building two warehouses totaling 1.7 million square feet on the 143-acre site.

But Monday, Township Planner Doreen Green outlined "Amendment 1" proposing new options:

  • 125-foot-tall, five-story "fulfillment center" no closer than 1,600 feet from the site's western border;
  • 40-foot-tall, three-story garage building;
  • 55-foot, two-story limit on other buildings on the site.

"The first plan is not scrapped," Board Attorney Mark Madaio said. "This amendment presents options."

Planning Board Chair Jeremiah Crean expressed reservations about the proposal, contending "this is a totally different project," and that the plans were vague. He questioned impact on traffic control, and the need for a parking garage, when the previous plan called for only ground-level parking. Member Megan Jankowski asked about power needs of the buildings.

"This sounds like a more intensive use to me," said Board Member Victoria Galow.

However, Madaio advised that their questions would be addressed at future site plan presentations. The limited purpose of the hearing was to rule on whether the proposal amendment was consistent with the master plan, nothing more.

"They are still limited to 35% maximum lot coverage," Green said. "We don't know yet what they're building, but planners are not involved in highway planning. That's done by the state."

SHERATON CLOSING Sheraton Crossroads in Mahwah is closing for good — and very soon. What we know

Board members reviewed master plan history to see what if any contradictions could be found. They noted that the maximum building height had not changed since the 250-foot-tall, 25-story hotel was built in 1987, taller than the proposed fulfillment center height. Uses were found to be similar in description to those already in the master plan.

Councilman David May spoke during the public hearing section of the meeting. He stated the original plan for the site was not just one 24-story building but "two more just like that." A previous proposal for a town village, 800 affordable housing units and 350,000 square feet of retail space was a more intense use.

"That's traffic," he said. "It's not a plan, just zoning. Height doesn't increase density."

The board eventually voted to declare the amendments "not inconsistent" with the master plan. Crean cast the only no vote. Mayor James Wysocki, a member of the board, was not present.
seoTitle: Sheraton Crossroads site: Mahwah NJ Planning Board decides future

title: Indian Hills High School hosts blind Turkish exchange student
fullText:
OAKLAND — Mert Ozer walked to the edge of the steps leading to the Indian Hills High School cafeteria last week and went down hands-free.

Not an easy feat for the blind exchange student from Istanbul, Turkey.

Leading the way to the school's guidance office, Mert stopped precisely at the wood door leading to the department. He explained that the door reflects sound differently than the cinderblock walls around it, so he knows where to stop.

"They brought me in before school started to walk me around so I could find my way," Mert said. "At first, I had an aide with me all the time, but I showed them I could get around on my own and that stopped."

Mert, 16, is finishing his junior year in the school. His student exchange year was facilitated through the American Field Service's Youth Exchange and Study program.

Youth Exchange and Study students come from predominantly Muslim countries to spend a year in an American public school as part of a cultural exchange. Of the 1,000 American Field Service students hosted by the program this school year, 171 came through the Youth Exchange and Study program. Two of those students listed a disability. Ten other schools were approached before Indian Hills agreed to take Mert.

"We've had exchange students before, but he was our first blind student," said Indian Hills Principal Gregory Vacca. "Our question was whether we could provide all he would need. Safety was a concern. We already had a relationship with the host parent, Ann Ford, so that helped. We had to start with a little trust on both sides."

For Ford, Mert is her eighth exchange student.

"Mert had to go to Oregon first for some training," Ford said. "I made a few adjustments. He didn't need bedside lamps, they just got in his way. I had to teach him the beeps on the microwave. But now he doesn't use his cane in the house. He gets around on his own."

Mert's English was good when he arrived, Ford said, however, she said he became more fluent and acquired something of a North Jersey accent as the year went on.

"He came out the first day after class with two students who had volunteered to make sure he found me," Ford said. "He did great."

It was a mutual learning experience for Mert and the faculty, according to Vacca. Mert had to demonstrate his keyboarding and computer skills using programs for the blind so teachers could understand how he could function in a mainstream classroom.

"Our students have MacBooks, and he had his own PC," said Guidance Counselor Susan Wiener. "He has an electronic device attached to his laptop that displays Braille. His biggest concern was that the constant presence of an aide made it difficult for him to interact with other students. It took awhile, but we figured it out. We even had to move him to a more challenging English class."

The teachers also improvised. Physics teacher Timothy Walkowich devised a tactile graph-drawing system using foam rubber sheets in various shapes so Mert could conceptualize how to chart results.

"Our physical education teachers had to create ways for Mert to participate in class, and the students were good about making sure he was included," Vacca said. "Everyone went above and beyond to find ways to help. The full community came together."

Mert's musical gifts provided another way for him to interact with his fellow students. Self-taught on the piano, Mert picked up the guitar in New Jersey, although he concedes he still needs help "where to put my fingers." His voice got him a lead role in the school's fall "Four Seasons" production, and the part of the Electric Skate in their spring musical "SpongeBob SquarePants."

"I had to dance, and didn't know if I could," Mert said. "Victoria Fox was our choreographer, and she was really helpful. I even had to learn how to bow."

His efforts earned him several awards at the year-end ceremonies on Wednesday. He was awarded The Instrumentalist Magazine Musicianship Award in band, the Chamber Choir Gold Pin in choir, the Musicianship Certificate for "Outstanding Soloist" and the Merit Certificate for Tenor in the school's Chamber Choir.

Ford said Mert has enjoyed a full year of music and travel, venturing into New York City with friends and attending several concerts including singers Andrea Bocelli, Billy Joel and Barry Manilow.

"We were up in the rafters at one concert, and the staff quietly came and invited us to take open orchestra seats because they could see he was blind," Ford said.

Among Mert's travels was a trip to Boston where he fell in love with its accessibility, its signaled traffic lights, and consequently its Berklee College of Music, which he hopes to attend after graduation in Turkey.

Just before a trip to prom with former exchange student Yazgi Akata, Mert presented the school with a "Medallion Member Recognition" certificate for providing him with a supportive educational community during his visit.

"What I learned was don't hesitate to ask for help," Mert said. "Direct communication is the most important. Don't assume earlier than you have to."

In that regard, Mert said for all his exposure to an American teen diet of hamburgers and pizza, there was something he was looking forward to back home.

"My mother is the best cook," Mert said.
seoTitle: Indian Hills High School hosts blind Turkish exchange student
