title: Development in Dover: 90 rental units going up on Route 46
fullText:
Construction is underway for a new "luxury" residential development on Route 46 in Dover that will bring 90 new rental units into the town.

Joint venture partners CrownPoint and Crossroads Companies are developing the .74-acre site with hopes of opening next year. The Town Council cleared the way for the deal in 2019 by declaring the property as an area in need of redevelopment. It later adopted a redevelopment plan in 2021 that permitted residential construction in a commercial zone.

Nine of the units will qualify as affordable housing that will count towards Dover's state-mandated affordable-housing construction quota. The rest will sell as market-rate "luxury" units, according to the developers.

The site was previously occupied for a few years by Hibachi Kitchen after functioning as the Attilio's Tavern sports bar and restaurant for several years. The building has now been unoccupied "for several years," according to the redevelopment plan.

Six stories plus rooftop deck

The new six-story building will include 5,000 square feet of "interior and exterior amenity spaces," including two stories of structured parking (117 spaces) below four stories of apartments and a rooftop deck, which the developers say is a first for Dover.

The developer has not listed additional specifics of the units and options. A note on their website says "More details soon."

'PILOT'-primed deal

The town in 2022 also granted the developers a "PILOT" program - or payment in lieu of taxes - that replaces conventional property taxes with a discounted payment plan. PILOTs have become a controversial topic in some towns, including Parsippany, with critics saying the plans cut school districts and local fire companies out of the line of direct tax revenue.

PILOT proponents, including Dover Mayor James Dodd, claim they are necessary and effective tools to entice developers to transform vacant or absolute properties into revenue-generating entities for the town.

"I think PILOTs are the only way do development now," Dodd said at a January council meeting while discussing another residential project on Blackwell Street. "There has to be a benefit for the municipality and the developer as well. It has to be a win-win for both."

PILOT programs given out over the past few years also typically include a provision to rent 10% of the new units as affordable housing to help satisfy a given town's state-mandated responsibility to build more affordable housing.
seoTitle: Development in Dover: 90 rental units going up on Route 46

title: Roxbury man whose body was recovered from Lake Hopatcong identified
fullText:
The body of an elderly Roxbury resident was recovered from Lake Hopatcong Monday morning, ending a multi-agency search that began Saturday night.

The Morris County Prosecutor's Office confirmed William Ryan, a 79-year-old resident of the Landing section, was found deceased at the southern end of the lake. He was last seen entering the lake at 7:30 p.m. Saturday "and did not return."

A search launched by the Roxbury Township Police Department, Morris County Sheriff’s Office, Morris County Prosecutor’s Office and New Jersey State Police Marine Unit was suspended Saturday night and resumed on Sunday morning. The Roxbury Fire Department also joined the search.

Water conditions and visibility hindered recovery efforts before the search was suspended again on Sunday night, a Morris County Prosecutor's Office spokesperson said. Search efforts included the use of a county submersible device, State Police divers, sonar and aviation.

The investigation continues but the circumstances of the incident are not considered suspicious, the prosecutor's office spokesperson said.

title: Police search for missing man last seen entering Lake Hopatcong
fullText:
Roxbury, Morris County and state authorities continued their search on Monday morning for an older man "who entered Lake Hopatcong and did not return" Saturday night.

Roxbury police confirmed on Monday there is a search and ongoing investigation of a possible drowning that began at 7:31 p.m. Saturday for a man believed to be in his 70s. The Roxbury Fire Department, New Jersey State Police and Morris County Sheriff's Department have joined the search.

Check back for updates to this story.

title: Morris mayors, Spadea to discuss 'redevelopment challenges' in Parsippany
fullText:
Parsippany Mayor James Barberio will be joined by other Morris County mayors Monday night for a public roundtable discussion of “redevelopment challenges,” including the developer tax breaks known as PILOTs and affordable-housing mandates.

The event will be moderated by Bill Spadea, the NJ101.5 radio host, conservative firebrand and rumored candidate for New Jersey governor next year. Mayors Thomas "Ace" Gallagher of Hanover, Joseph Pannullo of East Hanover, Mark Taylor of Florham Park and Michael Stanzilis of Mount Arlington are also scheduled to appear, Barberio's office announced on Tuesday.

The roundtable will be held from 6 to 8 p.m. at the Parsippany Sheraton hotel. There is no cost to attend, but space will be limited, and those who want to participate are encouraged to RSVP to action@parsippany.net, according to the Parsippany mayor's website.

PILOTs, affordable-housing stir controversy

With a glut of vacant office space, Parsippany has been at the forefront of local towns that have offered tax deals to developers willing to demolish the offices and replace them with new residential and commercial properties.

Proponents of the so-called PILOT programs (for "payments in lieu of taxes") say they incentivize builders and help towns solve another pressing issue, how to fulfill state-mandated, court-enforced quotas to provide affordable housing.

Critics, including some vocal members of the Parsippany Board of Education, say they are unnecessary perks for developers; they argue the discounted payments diminish tax revenues that would otherwise go to schools and fire districts.

Barberio has weathered criticism for championing more than half a dozen PILOTs in Parsippany over the last year. That climaxed with a council meeting in late December that drew 800 angry residents to sound off on the pending deals.

The Barberio-Spadea connection

Over the past year, Barberio also has connected with Spadea for several on-air interviews, including a spot last month in which the mayor criticized Parsippany Councilman Justin Musella, a fellow Republican, for Musella's pushback on PILOT deals and other initiatives. During Spadea's show, Barberio also took aim at another of his critics, Morris County Republican Chairwoman Laura Ali.

Musella chastised the mayor at a subsequent council meeting for taking their conflicts to the airwaves. Ali responded by branding Barberio - the county's only full-time mayor - as "the highest paid and least competent mayor in Morris County."

"Yes, I was on the radio this morning," Barberio shot back in May. "So what? I'm going to be on the radio a lot more. I can tell you that right now so I'll tell you when you can tune in and listen. I'm going to be out there a lot more. You're going to get the truth. You're going to get a lot of truth."

Whatever the political undercurrents, Gallagher, the Hanover mayor, said the roundtable was a chance to discuss a regional approach to problems he has struggled with for his 13 years in office.

"There's not a lot of dividing marks on these issues − affordable housing, redevelopment, flood remediation, our budgets," Gallagher said in an interview. "So we're trying to take a more regional approach."

More: 'New era' in Parsippany as massive housing complex opens for leasing. We got a look inside

Gallagher said he is all for affordable housing, but worries about the density of new residential projects, which typically consist of hundreds of of market-rate units along with more modestly priced housing.

"It's couched as a high-density housing discussion because of very serious (affordable housing) obligations coming in 2025," he said. "It's the density we're concerned about to get the affordable housing we need − the burdens it will put on our schools, our first responders."

title: Route 15 partially reopens to local traffic in Jefferson NJ
fullText:
After declaring a state of emergency in Jefferson over the closure of Route 15 South, Mayor Eric Wilsusen said that one lane of the highway has been reopened for residents to access some local homes and businesses.

The state Department of Transportation agreed to the partial reopening on Thursday but only for local traffic, Wilsusen told the Daily Record. He added on his Facebook page that only the "top portion" of the area affected by the shutdown would now be accessible, though efforts were underway to expand that by Friday.

The state abruptly closed the road on Tuesday after a bridge over the Rockaway River near Berkshire Valley Road failed a safety inspection. That has led to massive delays for the thousands of travelers in Morris and Sussex counties who use the highway every day, and problems for local businesses and residents dealing with the traffic detoured through their streets.

Route 15 northbound through the township remains open.

While Wilsusen had no word on a long-term solution, he told the Daily Record that the DOT would hold a conference call at 9 a.m. Friday with local officials to offer an update on the state's plan.

Jefferson declares state of emergency

"I have been emphasizing that there is no other option than creating a temporary structure, detours on my local roads cannot be a sustainable option." the mayor added.

On Wednesday, Wilsusen said he had declared a local state of emergency, which he said would increase the town's ability to regulate traffic and deal with expenses created by the shutdown.

"It does not give us a lot of authority, but we are incurring expenses due to this closure," Wilsusen said in another update on Facebook.

DOT plans website for Route 15 commuters

The DOT is promising to release more information to help travelers, state Senator Parker Space said on his Facebook page with fellow 24th District legislators Dawn Fantasia and Michael Inganamort. The district includes parts of Morris County and all of Sussex.

"The DOT is establishing a website where commuters and residents can find daily project updates and other pertinent information," they wrote, promising to notify the public as soon as the website is up and running.

The legislators said they held an online meeting with state officials and local leaders to press for a solution. "Knowing that upwards of 60 percent of Sussex County residents commute out of the county for work, they stressed the severity of the situation for our commuters and advocated for an opening as quickly as possible," according to their statement.

More: When will Route 15 reopen? Here's the latest as Morris, Sussex drivers battle huge delays

Local residents 'terrified' by speeding traffic

Meanwhile, commuters and residents are frustrated. The detours are causing speeding and reckless driving around local roads.

"The worst part is the angry drivers absolutely flying up the side streets, thinking they've found some kind of shortcut, only to be met with even more traffic as they stand on their horn," one Facebook user wrote under Mayor Wilsusen's post. "I don't even have kids but I'm terrified for my neighbors kids."

The state had planned to reduce Route 15 Southbound to one lane this week as part of an $11.6 million replacement of the bridge. But the entire roadway was shut down on Tuesday afternoon after the failed inspection.

The DOT hasn't yet given a timetable for the emergency repairs.

"Work continues on the project to replace the 124-year-old Route 15 southbound bridge over the Rockaway River, which began last summer," the department said in a statement Wednesday. "Engineers are conducting a structural evaluation. The bridge will remain closed and detoured at this time."Email: NFlanagan@gannett.com

title: Route 15 partially reopens to local traffic in Jefferson NJ
fullText:
After declaring a state of emergency in Jefferson over the closure of Route 15 South, Mayor Eric Wilsusen said that one lane of the highway has been reopened for residents to access some local homes and businesses.

The state Department of Transportation agreed to the partial reopening on Thursday but only for local traffic, Wilsusen told the Daily Record. He added on his Facebook page that only the "top portion" of the area affected by the shutdown would now be accessible, though efforts were underway to expand that by Friday.

The state abruptly closed the road on Tuesday after a bridge over the Rockaway River near Berkshire Valley Road failed a safety inspection. That has led to massive delays for the thousands of travelers in Morris and Sussex counties who use the highway every day, and problems for local businesses and residents dealing with the traffic detoured through their streets.

Route 15 northbound through the township remains open.

While Wilsusen had no word on a long-term solution, he told the Daily Record that the DOT would hold a conference call at 9 a.m. Friday with local officials to offer an update on the state's plan.

Jefferson declares state of emergency

"I have been emphasizing that there is no other option than creating a temporary structure. Detours on my local roads cannot be a sustainable option." the mayor added.

On Wednesday, Wilsusen said he had declared a local state of emergency, which he said would increase the town's ability to regulate traffic and deal with expenses created by the shutdown.

"It does not give us a lot of authority, but we are incurring expenses due to this closure," Wilsusen said in another update on Facebook.

DOT plans website for Route 15 commuters

The DOT is promising to release more information to help travelers, state Senator Parker Space said on his Facebook page with fellow 24th District legislators Dawn Fantasia and Michael Inganamort. The district includes Roxbury, nearby parts of Morris County and all of Sussex.

"The DOT is establishing a website where commuters and residents can find daily project updates and other pertinent information," they wrote, promising to notify the public as soon as the website is up and running.

The legislators said they held an online meeting with state officials and local leaders to press for a solution. "Knowing that upwards of 60 percent of Sussex County residents commute out of the county for work, they stressed the severity of the situation for our commuters and advocated for an opening as quickly as possible," according to their statement.

More: When will Route 15 reopen? Here's the latest as Morris, Sussex drivers battle huge delays

Local residents 'terrified' by speeding traffic

Meanwhile, commuters and residents are frustrated. The detours are causing speeding and reckless driving around local roads.

"The worst part is the angry drivers absolutely flying up the side streets, thinking they've found some kind of shortcut, only to be met with even more traffic as they stand on their horn," one Facebook user wrote under Mayor Wilsusen's post. "I don't even have kids but I'm terrified for my neighbors kids."

The state had planned to reduce Route 15 Southbound to one lane this week as part of an $11.6 million replacement of the bridge. But the entire roadway was shut down on Tuesday afternoon after the failed inspection.

The DOT hasn't yet given a timetable for the emergency repairs.

"Work continues on the project to replace the 124-year-old Route 15 southbound bridge over the Rockaway River, which began last summer," the department said in a statement Wednesday. "Engineers are conducting a structural evaluation. The bridge will remain closed and detoured at this time."Email: NFlanagan@gannett.com

title: Bob Zufall was NJ's humanitarian role model
fullText:
Dr. Bob Zufall’s retired colleagues couldn’t turn him down in 1990 when he asked for volunteers at the modest, free health clinic he was creating in Dover.

They didn’t know that his one-night-a-week operation would grow into an award-winning, seven-county behemoth that now serves some 45,000 uninsured or under-insured patients who otherwise would swamp hospital emergency rooms. But they knew their old friend and his wife sometimes flew to South America to help treat the impoverished.

How could they say no to New Jersey’s version of Albert Schweitzer?

It might seem like a stretch to compare the self-described country doctor, who died in March at age 99, to the towering humanitarian and Nobel Peace Prize winner who — in his thirties — sacrificed nearly all human comforts to treat natives at a clinic in equatorial Africa. At 65, Zufall was a comfortably retired urologist when he began offering free, primary-care treatment to the poor in a church basement a few miles from the Mountain Lakes home where he and his wife, Kay, raised five children.

Unlike Schweitzer, who endured brutal conditions including imprisonment during his early days as a missionary doctor, Zufall’s mission entailed little personal sacrifice. But like Schweitzer, he felt impelled to fill a need that few others fully recognized at the time.

“There’s a lot of poor folks right here,” he recalled telling Kay when she suggested a return to Peru.

Although Morris County consistently ranks among the nation’s 10 wealthiest counties, its poverty level was more than noticeable to physicians who treated immigrants and other non-English-speaking patients in hospitals such as Dover General. Now part of St. Clare’s Medical Center, that’s where Zufall practiced for 36 years, a period that marked a sharp rise in New Jersey’s Hispanic population, especially in Dover where Latinos now account for 70% of the town’s residents.

“How about staying in Dover?” he said, knowing full well that his wife would agree.

The ideal helpmate

Luckily, Kathryn Schwindt Zufall was a no-nonsense organizer who recruited volunteers to help staff the little office, as well as local donors who supplemented the coins and dollar bills that patients dropped into a little box.

“Everyone knew she’d never take no for an answer,” said my wife, Susan, who — full disclosure — was a public relations consultant for the health center for several years.

Watching the little Dover Free Clinic morph into the larger Dover Community Clinic, we couldn’t help but admire the generous, self-effacing doctor who had a kind word for everyone, and the tough, onetime teacher who once convinced a local merchant that sending his used furniture to her pet project would do much more good than leaving it for the garbage hauler.

Kay, who died in 2014, was especially good at cultivating friends in high places — often unbeknownst to her modest husband. As Dr. Bob noted in a 2019 interview, state health department staff surprised him in 1971 with a phone call asking for a tour of his clinic. Soon he was shaking hands with the health commissioner himself.

“This guy, Bruce Siegel, came and I was pretty embarrassed,” he recalled, “I said, ‘This isn’t much of a place. It’s just a little thing,’ and he says, ‘I like it; I’ll give you $100,000 a year!’”

In its news columns, The New York Times placed the figure at $97,500 — enough to pay a full-time nurse, a part-time social worker and some supplies, but not nearly enough to sustain what was becoming a six-day-a-week operation swamped mostly with non-English-speaking immigrants, the unemployed and the working poor.

As Albert Schweitzer knew in the early 20th century, financing a fledgling clinic took much more. A renowned lecturer, theologian and organist, he managed to raise capital by performing at concerts and lecture halls throughout Europe and America. In the late 20th century, the Zufalls lacked that sort of star power.

They didn’t realize it then, but their timing was nevertheless exquisite.

Federal healthcare reforms

Starting in the 1990s, federal legislation began recognizing centers like theirs as important safety-net providers specifically designed for underserved urban and rural communities. Regulations demanded that primary-care patients could not be denied treatment -- even if unable to pay. Once accepted as a Federally Qualified Health Center, a community clinic was eligible for substantial planning grants and operational funding.

“FQHCs are the wave of the future,” Zufall proclaimed. “They do a good job and… they regulate us closely.”

But as the couple moved into their eighties and Kay grew ill, could they continue to manage their brainchild under the heavy bureaucratic requirements that government support would surely bring?

Schweitzer faced similar challenges. His brainchild eventually included 70 buildings and 500 beds, but he never installed phones, running water or modern electricity. He never relinquished control, and after his death at age 90 in 1965, critics called him a racist, which sharply conflicted with his oft-quoted “Reverence for Life” beliefs that all lives deserve respect.

By contrast, the founder of the little Dover operation stepped back gracefully, “so the clinic could be sustained and flourish,” said Eva Turbiner, a veteran healthcare professional and business-development consultant who became the center’s president and chief executive officer.

But Dr. Bob was still on the job — full-time.

Remaining a board member, he embraced Turbiner’s plans for expanding the center’s reach throughout northwestern New Jersey -- to Hackettstown, Flemington, Morristown, Newton, West Orange, Bridgewater and Plainsboro. Besides additional geography, these satellites targeted new categories of need including farm workers, veterans, diabetics, public housing residents and the homeless.'

Obituary: NJ 'visionary' who founded Zufall Health network for low-income patients dies at 99

Cash to reinforce the dream

“He put his money where his mouth was,” Turbiner told a crowd of 160 who attended Dr. Bob’s memorial service in April. “In addition to endowing the clinic at its founding, he put up the down payment for a new headquarters in Dover and he was the first major donor to support construction of our West Orange office.”

In 2009, he and Kay were given the New Jersey version of the prestigious Jefferson humanitarian award for their volunteerism. It wasn’t the only time the center received top honors. Pharmaceutical giants such as Becton Dickinson and foundations such as Direct Relief, which specializes in humanitarian aid, began taking notice of the once-tiny clinic that kept producing innovations for reaching vulnerable people from their strategically located offices and specially equipped mobile vans.

“You win every damn award we think up,” said Direct Relief’s president, Thomas Tighe, at a fundraiser for the center in 2021, “and it’s because Zufall is at the top of the top in terms of all the things that matter.”

Such compliments tended to embarrass the center’s founder. He bristled, for example, at a proposal to rename the center for him and his wife. The board summarily overrode him.

“I was just trying to be humble,” he later told Fran Palm, who succeeded Turbiner last year as the center’s top executive.

‘Rock star’ recognition

Nevertheless, whenever he visited any of his center’s 10 clinical sites, neither humility nor advancing age dampened the adulation that the staff showered on their namesake -- even though many were meeting him for the first time.

“They treated him like a rock star!” said Turbiner. “He was our chief cheerleader.”

Remarkably, as he neared the centennial of his birth this year, Dr. Bob remained active in nearly all health center functions including three-hour board meetings -- often via Zoom -- over policy issues that might induce sleep in a man half his age.

“Here was this 99-year-old studying compliance-risk assessment analyses, reviewing by-laws, sliding fee schedules and financial reports — and loving it!” fellow board member Bill Shuler recalled at the memorial service before pausing o ask the audience: “What are you doing with your spare time?”

Dr. Bob did much more than cheer. He was a gifted role model who used the time he had left to set an example -- a term that a famous Nobel laureate once defined this way: “Example is not the main thing in influencing others; it is the only thing.”

Unlike Albert Schweitzer, Robert Bunger Zufall might not have qualified for the Nobel Peace Prize, but his medical legacy and the way he achieved it surely rival the achievements of the 1952 winner. Others have founded hospitals and made huge financial contributions. Many have volunteered their medical talents or sat on boards of directors. Some have even saved lives and improved the health of tens upon thousands of vulnerable people.

But as Fran Palm noted, few, if any, did all that for more than three decades for no pay AFTER formal retirement at 65 — simply for the privilege of helping others.

“He’s the kind of person I’d like to be in the last years of my life,” she said.

John Cichowski is the retired Road Warrior columnist for northjersey.com. He can be reached at jwcichowski@optonline.net

title: Glen Ridge NJ girls lacrosse edges Mountain Lakes in state final
fullText:
BASKING RIDGE − Mountain Lakes returned to the Group 1 state girls lacrosse final, hoping to grab the state title that alluded them a season ago.

In a back and forth affair, the Lakers came up one goal shy, dropping a 9-8 final to Glen Ridge on Saturday at Ridge High School.

"It was a great game," coach Alyssa Sebesto said. "It stinks that there had to be a loser and it stinks that it had to be us, but you can't ask for a better final."

Mountain Lakes controlled possession in the first quarter with goals by Kayla Plotts and Kaylin Oey giving the Lakers a 2-1 advantage after 12 minutes. Glen Ridge responded with a strong second quarter to take a 5-4 lead into the half.

Mountain Lakes trailed by multiple goals early in the third quarter, but goals by Plotts and Julia Petersen tied the game 6-6 with 6:25 to go in the third. Petersen added another goal, her second of the quarter and third of the game, to give Mountain Lakes a 7-6 lead with 5:15 left in the third.

Tied 8-8 after three quarters, possessions became long and important in the final 12 minutes. Glen Ridge spent nearly the first three minutes of the fourth quarter on a possession, resulting in what turned out to be the game-winning goal.

Mountain Lakes had opportunities down the stretch with possession for nearly all of the final 90 seconds of regulation. Petersen came inches away from a game-tying goal in the final seconds with a shot that clanged off the far post. A turnover with seven seconds left gave Mountain Lakes one last attempt to tie, but the shot went high above the net as time expired.

"Julia had the hot hand today and I was trying to get her the ball in the stick, but unfortunately she hit the pipe," Sebesto said. "You can't ask for a better shot."

The Lakers excelled under Sebesto, a first-year head coach and a Mountain Lakes alum who was part of the program's last state title back in 2014. With a final record of 11-10, Sebesto credited her team for returning to the state final for the second straight season despite a rough 2-6 start through a difficult schedule.

"From where we started to get here, it says something," Sebesto said. "This wasn't really on my radar when we started how we did. To make it here is great. I got to enjoy it as a player when I won 10 years ago and it would have been nice to win it again. We'll put the work in and have to come back again next year."

Mountain Lakes' final three losses this season all came to some of the top teams in the state. In addition to Saturday's loss to Glen Ridge, the Lakers lost to Group 4 finalist Morristown in the Morris County tournament semifinals on May 8, and also dropped a game to North Group 3 finalist Morris Knolls two days later.

title: Morris Knolls softball claims second straight state sectional title
fullText:
DENVILLE – All Julia Fox was thinking was to keep it simple.

With leadoff batter and teammate Taylor Heinemann standing on third base with one out in the first inning, the Morris Knolls sophomore was focused on hitting a shot deep enough to the outfield to help her team in the biggest game of the season.

Facing a 2-1 hitter’s count, Fox’s sacrifice fly to right field plated Heinemann in what turned out to be the only run of the game to lift Morris Knolls to a 1-0 victory over rival Morris Hills on Saturday in the NJSIAA North 1, Group 3 final. It’s the Golden Eagles second straight sectional title.

Senior pitcher Leah Kleczkowski spun a three-hit, complete game shutout with six strikeouts to lead the Denville school to its sixth straight win.

Morris Knolls will host Randolph in a Group 3 semifinal on Tuesday. Randolph defeated North Hunterdon, 8-3 on Saturday in the North 2, Group 3 final.

“I was looking for a sacrifice fly. I just knew that I didn’t want to pop up in the infield because I knew Taylor and that run could be really crucial,” Fox said. “It’s a great feeling to win again. The whole team plays really well together. It’s not too often you get to experience something like this.”

Heinemann came out swinging in the bottom half of the first inning and reached second base when she laced a fly ball to left field on a 2-1 count that tailed away and ended up scored an error. She then stole third just ahead of Fox’s plate appearance.

“I just made sure that I got back to the base in time and run as fast to home and make sure I was safe,” Heinemann said. “We’ve put in a lot of work this season and it’s nice to win it again.”

The Golden Eagles could only string together two hits - singles from Makayla Rady in the third and Hailey Poskonka in the fifth - but tight defense and a big-game effort by Kleczkowski was enough to hold it down.

Morris Hills (15-13) threatened in the sixth inning when its first two batters reached base, giving the Scarlet Knights runners on first and second with no outs. But the Golden Eagles defense buckled down and Kleczkowski induced the next two batters to pop up in the infield and a ground out.

“I’m not surprised it was only a one-run game. I wish it was bigger, but I knew it was going to be a tight game. They [Morris Hills] always put up a good fight. I’m glad we won,” Kleczkowski  said. “Winning by a run is still a win. We’ve prepared all season for this moment. It’s a great feeling knowing the hard work is paying off.”

Morris Hills pitcher Zoe Turner was impressive, going six innings on two hits and no runs.

What it means

Morris Knolls (23-4) is state sectional champions for the second straight year. They’ve reached a sectional final three straight times.

In their four postseason games, the Golden Eagles have only surrendered one run. Morris Knolls has outscored its opponents, 21-1 with three shutouts.,

The Golden Eagles face county and division rival Randolph (20-8) next in a Group 3 semifinal on Tuesday. Morris Knolls defeated the Rams twice during the regular season and have outscored them, 14-3.

“This year we’re just a little more experienced compared to last year. We’re just a year older,” Morris Knolls coach Keith Heinemann said. “Leah has been fantastic this whole tournament. Their [Morris Hills] pitching did a great job and kept us off the bases. We’re still alive.”

They said it

“Whenever we play [Morris] Hills, no matter the sport, it’s always an intense game. Our whole motto this season is ‘nothing is given, everything is earned.’ We knew we had to come out, compete and do our jobs. We knew it was going to be a battle. I felt prepared and confident because I have a very strong defense with good hitters behind me. It’s my senior year and you always want to end on a good note. I knew I could do it and I’m happy coach believed in me.” - Kleczkowski

“We knew today was going to be different than the last time we played them. Their coaches do a great job and they have some really good young talent. Their pitcher has been lights out all tournament, so we expected the challenge.” - Keith Heinemann

title: Morris Catholic NJ softball wins fourth straight sectional title
fullText:
DENVILLE -- A fourth North Non-Public B title for Morris Catholic was sealed on a four bagger.

Kate Heslin’s walk-off grand slam was the coup de grace as Morris Catholic took down St. Mary 14-4 in six innings Monday afternoon to earn another sectional crown.

“If we’re going to have anybody with a chance to finish the game, you couldn’t design it any better than Kate Heslin, there is not a better hitter in New Jersey,” said Crusaders coach Nick DeGennaro. “We’ve had a lot of ups and downs, and we’re playing a lot of young kids that don’t know what this grind is. I am really proud of them. There’s a lot of character on this team.”

Heslin finished the day 2-4 with two runs scored. Sophomore pitcher Sofia Reisinger was 2-2 with two RBIs and also took control in the last two innings in the circle.

“We had one bad inning and that’s what we were trying to work on all year, limiting the walks and the errors,” said St. Mary coach Sarah Piening. “They were the better team today.”

What It Means

The Crusaders (19-8) won the Non-Public B title in 2021 and 2022, but lost to St. Joe’s of Hammonton 7-1 in the final in 2023. They’ll face the Wildcats again for the state title Thursday at Kean.

St. Joe’s of Hammonton features East Carolina commitment Ava Fisher in the circle.

“I think this team, the challenge, every time you throw a challenge in front of them, they’ve stepped up every time,” said DeGennaro. “I think facing St. Joe’s will bring out the best in us. It’s going to be a challenge. I will think about them tomorrow.”

St. Mary became a contender again in North Jersey with the school absorbing the bulk of the talented Immaculate Conception team when that school closed.

“It was a great season overall, I think our program is headed in a great direction,” said Piening. “I am very proud of our team. We had a senior transfer and a junior transfer who did a lot for us this year. I am looking forward to the direction that the program is heading in.”

Two Outs In the Fifth

The teams traded punches in the early innings. Morris Catholic took a 2-0 lead in the second inning, only to see St. Mary rally back for two in the top of the third. Morris Catholic answered with two in their half of the third.

It was 4-3 Morris Catholic with two outs in the bottom of the fifth when the game swung for Morris Catholic. Reisinger started things off with a double, then Natalie Carovillano followed with an RBI double. An error, a misplay and a couple of walks kept the inning going and St. Mary brought in a new pitcher.

Marielle Balonze laced a two-run single down the right field line to make it 10-3 and take all the wind out of St Mary’s sails.

“I knew they would come to play,” said DeGennaro. “The graduating seniors were kids that gave us a dogfight two years ago from IC. They have a lot of energy. I fully expected that this was going to be a dogfight, but I thought when they made a pitching change and we started getting on base, we played against her last year and we felt good about hitting against her.”

They Said It

“I think we figured out a lot of things about ourselves,” said DeGennaro. “I think the Mount game, a 2-1 loss, was one of our best games we played all year. We made some great plays in the outfield that game, but I think that it was knowing that who we see, they’re not better than we’ve already seen.”

title: Morris Knolls NJ softball returning to Group 3 state final
fullText:
ROCKAWAY − The Morris Knolls softball team has thought about the loss in last season's Group 3 state final for nearly a year.

On Friday, the Golden Eagles will return to the final for a chance at a state title. Morris Knolls rallied in the middle innings and fended off a furious comeback in the seventh to win, 5-3, for the program's second straight trip to a group final, and fourth overall.

Randolph jumped out to a 1-0 lead on a Cassidy Smith home run in the top of the first. Morris Knolls saw five runners reach base the next three innings, but was unable to plate a tying run. In the bottom of the fourth, senior Anna Chominsky broke through with a leadoff double and advanced to third on an errant throw. Chominsky scored on an infield hit by Hailey Poskonka to tie the game 1-1. An inning later, Chominsky delivered again with a two-run single to put Morris Knolls ahead for the first time at 3-1.

Randolph respond as junior Autumn Liebhauser slugged a solo home run to cut the lead in half in the top of the sixth. Liebhauser's 16th home run of the season tied her for the state lead and also marked her 100th career hit.

The Golden Eagles continued to push in the bottom of the sixth as Taylor Heinemann legged out a double, stole third base and scored on a squeeze by Sofia Cruz, who later came around to score and give Morris Knolls a 5-2 lead.

Those last three outs were hard to come by as Randolph senior Samantha Niewiarowski poked a solo home run over the left field fence, her first varsity home run in her final high school at-bat. The next three Rams all reached base to load the bases with one out. But senior Leah Kleczkowski struck out the next two batters, including Liebhauser for the game's final out.

Morris Knolls moves on to Friday's Group 3 state final at Ivy Hill Park against Steinert, which beat Moorestown in Tuesday's other Group 3 state semifinal. Steinert defeated Morris Knolls in last season's Group 3 final. Morris Knolls has not won a group title since the program's lone championship in 1980.

Check back soon for more.

title: Jack Alexy: Swimmer and Delbarton grad from Mendham, NJ, qualifies for Olympics
fullText:
Make room for more Morris County swimmers on Team USA.

Jack Alexy of Mendham has qualified for the 400-meter freestyle relay on Wednesday night in Indianapolis.

Alexy, a 6-foot-8 rising senior at Cal-Berkeley, finished second in the 100-meter free final in 47.47, nine hundredths of a second out of first.

"It's so awesome," Alexy said on the live television broadcast. "This experience is really surreal, especially coming in here tonight. There's quite a bit of relief as well. I'm happy to go to Paris with these guys."

Alexy had earned the first seed in the 100 free at USA Swimming's Olympic Trials. In the prelim on Tuesday morning, Alexy finished in 47.08 seconds – the second-fastest time in the world this season.

Alexy joins Nic Fink of Morristown on USA Swimming's Olympic squad. Fink, a 30-year-old heading to his second Games, qualified in the 100 breaststroke on Sunday night.

Get to know Jack Alexy

At the NCAA Championships in March, Alexy finished second in the 200 free (school-record 1:29.75) and third in the 50 free (personal-best 18.38) and 100 free (school-record 40.59). He had earned five All-American honors as a sophomore, placing second in the 100 free, fourth in the 100 back and sixth in the 50 free as Cal won back-to-back NCAA team titles.

Alexy made his senior Team USA debut at the 2023 World Championships, winning gold in the 400 medley relay. He had competed at the 2021 Olympic Trials shortly after graduating from Delbarton, finishing 17th in the 50 and 33rd in the 100 backstroke.

More: Swimmer Nic Fink of Morristown qualifies for Paris Olympics with victory at U.S. trials

Alexy is a four-time NJSIAA Meet of Champions winner, capturing the 50 free and 100 back as a freshman and the 50 and 100 free in 2020 to cap his junior season.

What's next for Jack Alexy

Alexy began competition in the 50-meter freestyle on Thursday morning, posting a 21.74 – the second-fastest time in prelims, seven hundredths behind the leaders. He will be the No. 3 qualifier in the 50 free final, which is scheduled for approximately 8 p.m. Friday.

title: Wave's Kristen McNabb back home in NJ for NWSL showdown with Gotham
fullText:
Kristen McNabb's fan club will probably be easy to find when the San Diego Wave visits Gotham FC for a National Women's Soccer League match on Wednesday at Red Bull Arena. Just look for the crowd of matching T-shirts, quite possibly in the Wave's trademark hot pink.

Her older sister, Rutgers alumna Lindsey McNabb Hover, will likely be leading the cheers.

As the Wave's starting left back, Kristen McNabb, who grew up in Montville, isn't used to that kind of attention. She joked about her far more famous teammate, "If they notice me behind Alex Morgan, that'll be pretty cool. I'll take it."

But McNabb admitted to getting "an extra driving force" from having friends and family in the stands, something that rarely happens at San Diego's home matches.

The Wave and visiting Gotham played to a 1-1 draw on May 12. San Diego (3-4-5) is ninth among 14 NWSL teams, with no road wins.

"(New Jersey) does still hold a special place in my heart," said McNabb, whose sister's family lives in West Orange. "It's always nice to look up into the stands and see my loved ones."

Proud to be (sort of) a Jersey girl

McNabb was born in Newport Beach, California, but the family relocated through Louisiana; Massachusetts; Montgomery, New Jersey; and back to California, as dad Mark McNabb – an automotive executive and former NSCAA Division III All-American at Babson – was transferred.

The McNabbs moved back to New Jersey, settling in Montville in Morris County, when Lindsey was going to be a sophomore and Kristen a seventh grader. Though Lindsey McNabb played one year of high school soccer in Irvine, California, and then one at Montville after the family relocated, Kristen McNabb focused on the club game at Players Development Academy.

Kristen McNabb mainly played center back and defensive midfield, twice captaining PDA Charge to second place in the Elite Club National League. But she tore her left ACL in the spring of her senior year, and sat out her freshman season at Virginia. She appeared in 19 matches as a sophomore before tearing her right ACL.

McNabb started all but one match in her last two college seasons, usually with her parents – who had moved again, this time to Washington D.C. – in the stands.

More: Meet the 17 New Jersey soccer players in NWSL as 2024 season begins

"Unless Kristen McNabb plays for you, you don't understand the quality of player she is and the quality of person she is," said longtime Virginia women's soccer coach Steve Swanson, who recently visited McNabb and two other alumnae in San Diego. "She does all the little things that are so important to winning. ... She's the definition of a professional. You know what you're going to get day in and day out, and they're going to bring it every single day. It's going to be real high quality, maximum effort, maximum focus."

Go west, young player

A fan of the East Coast, McNabb was selected by Seattle in the fourth round in 2017. She had two goals and two assists in 87 matches (6,017 minutes) with the Reign. San Diego picked McNabb in the expansion draft in December 2021. She's played 4,584 minutes in 54 games for the Wave, who earned the 2023 NWSL Shield with the best regular-season record.

But physical issues have continued to follow McNabb, who missed the second half of last season with a hip injury.

"It gave me perspective," she said of her many injuries. "I have a tendency to be very hard on myself, very intense. I like to win. I like to play. When I had a bad game as a kid, I was a miserable, terrible human, to my parents mainly. Getting that experience when you can't play, that sucks even more.

"As an older, veteran player, when that happens, you remember to count your blessings that you're in the situation you're in," said McNabb, who turned 30 in April. "At the end of the day, I love to play soccer. That's the ultimate goal: to get back on the field."

Veteran McNabb finding a home

Though McNabb recalled going to San Diego Spirit games with her family when they lived in California back in the early 2000s, she hadn't seriously considered turning pro while growing up. The Women's United Soccer Association survived only from April 2001 to September 2003. Women's Professional Soccer launched in 2007, followed by the National Women's Soccer League in 2012 – her freshman year in college.

She's adjusted to her role as a veteran, though San Diego coach Casey Stoney admitted McNabb is usually a quiet leader. Stoney is hoping McNabb will be more consistent in her third season, settling in at left back.

"When Kristen is fit, healthy and confident, she's one of the best left backs in the league," Stoney said. "She plays simple, plays quick. I'd like to get her more in the attacking third. To get her higher up is a key thing. ... She's got steely determination to do well."

title: Fourth of July fireworks shows and more North Jersey things to do
fullText:
Independence Day will be here before we know it, so it's time to start planning how you'd like to celebrate. And, while attending a family gathering or a backyard barbecue could be fun, there's nothing quite like ringing in the Fourth of July with some fireworks, parades, festivals and more.

Because North Jersey has celebrations taking place in every corner of the region, we've compiled a list of the currently scheduled events to make your life easier.

Here's a look at the Fourth of July events and firework shows taking place across North Jersey in 2024, by day:

June 26

  • Montville 4th of July Celebration. From June 26 through June 28, Montville will be hosting their annual 4th of July celebration events. Each day features different attractions, including food and beer trucks, carnival rides, live entertainment, a car show and fireworks. Hours: Open 5 to 10 p.m. each day. Go: Montville Township High School, 100 Horseneck Road, Montville.

June 27

  • Edgewater Independence Day Fireworks. Live music, food trucks, kids activities and fireworks on June 27. Bring a chair or blanket. Parking is limited, so attendees are encouraged to use the free River Road shuttle bus. The rain date is June 30. Hours: 6 to 10 p.m. Fireworks begin at approximately 9:20. Go: Veterans Field, 1057-1165 River Road, Edgewater.
  • Fair Lawn Fireworks Show. Fair Lawn will be hosting their annual fireworks show on June 27. In addition to fireworks, there will be food vendors and live music for guests to enjoy. Tickets for the pre-fireworks festivities are $5 for children under 12 and seniors, $7 for adults and $25 for a family of five. Hours: Gates for the event open at 6:45 p.m., and fireworks begin at sundown. Go: Memorial Park, Berdan Avenue and 1st Street, Fair Lawn.

June 28

  • Verona Fourth of July Fireworks. Verona's Fourth of July event on June 28 will include a night full of dancing with a DJ and other live entertainment, as well as a fireworks show at dusk. Hours: Starts at 7 pm. Go: Verona Community Center, 880 Bloomfield Ave., Verona.
  • Lake Hopatcong Annual Fourth of July Fireworks. The Lake Hopatcong Yacht Club will be hosting their annual July 4th fireworks on June 28 on the main lake of Lake Hopatcong. Parking will be available on Bertrand Island for residents and members only. Hours: 9:30 to 10:30 p.m. Go: 75 North Bertrand Road, Mount Arlington.
  • The Essex County Free Summer Concert Series will include a free performance in Newark by the New Jersey Symphony Orchestra, featuring a fireworks display. The program will feature a medley of classics, Broadway themes and patriotic favorites; as well as John Williams’ Liberty Fanfare, John Philip Sousa’s Atlantic City Pageant March and other Jersey treasures. Hours: Concert begins at 7:30 p.m. Go: The Great Lawn at Branch Brook Park, Heller Parkway. In case of rain, the concert will be relocated to the Jim Wise Theatre in Kupfrian Hall on Summit Street on the campus of NJIT.

June 29

  • Morris Plains Family Day and Fireworks. The annual Morris Plains Family Day will be held at Morris Plains Community Park on June 29, featuring food, activities and entertainment. Then, their July 4th fireworks show will take place after sundown. Hours: Family Day begins at 5 p.m., and the fireworks begin around 9:30 p.m. Go: 51 Jim Fear Dr., Morris Plains.
  • Bloomingdale July 4th Fireworks. Bloomingdale will host their annual July 4th fireworks show on June 29 at Walter T. Bergen School. The event will also include food and rides. Hours: Starts at 6 p.m. Go: 225 Glenwild Ave., Bloomingdale.
  • Montague Day and July 4th Fireworks. Montague Day on June 29 will feature the Miss Montague Contest, an animal exhibit, live entertainment, a cornhole tournament, a dunk tank, vendors, food, fireworks after dark and more. Hours: The event starts at 4 p.m., and the fireworks begin after dark. Go: Montague Town Hall, 227 Clover Road, Montague.

June 30

  • Paramus 4th of July Fireworks Show. Paramus will be hosting their annual 4th of July fireworks show on June 30. Prior to the fireworks show, there will be live entertainment and food vendors. Hours: The time of the event is to be determined. Go: Cliff Gennarelli Sports Complex, Garden State Plaza Parkway, Paramus.
  • Paterson Food Truck Festival and Fireworks. Visitors are invited to enjoy food from local businesses at a food truck festival, followed by July 4th fireworks on June 30. Hours: Starts at 5 p.m. Go: Great Falls Welcome Center, 65 McBride Ave. Extension, Paterson.

July 1

  • Hanover Township Patriotic Celebration. Hanover Township is holding their 2024 Patriotic Celebration, which will feature food trucks, live music, games, face painting, balloon art and fireworks. Hours: 6 to 10 p.m. Go: Hanover Township Municipal Complex, 1000 Route 10, Whippany.
  • Cedar Grove Annual Fireworks Display. Cedar Grove is hosting their annual Fourth of July fireworks display and celebration event, which features a live DJ, a balloon artist, a patriotic obstacle course, crafts and refreshments. Hours: Starts at 7 p.m. Go: Panther Park Field, 118 W Bradford Ave., Cedar Grove.
  • City of Englewood's Fireworks Show. Mayor Michael Wildes and the Englewood City Council invite you to the City's fireworks celebration on July 1. The rain date is July 2. Hours: 7:30 p.m. Go: Front lawn of Dwight Morrow High School, 274 Knickerbocker Road.

July 2

  • Essex County Free Summer Concert Series and Fireworks. Listen Men of Soul perform soul and R&B music, and enjoy a fireworks display. Hours: Begins at 7:30 p.m. Go: Weequahic Park, Elizabeth and Meeker avenues in Newark.
  • Mountain Lakes July 4th Fireworks. A festive July 4th fireworks show will take place July 2 over Mountain Lake, and Island Beach will be open for viewing. Hours: Starts at 9 p.m. Go: 276 Boulevard, Mountain Lakes.

July 3

  • Dover July 4th Fireworks and Celebration. Dover will be hosting a July 4th celebration with food, activities, live entertainment and fireworks on July 3. Hours: Starts at 6 p.m. Go: 302 E. McFarlan St., Dover.
  • Glen Rock Pops Celebrates Nation’s Birthday. The Pops Orchestra goes patriotic on July 3 with a free concert on the lawn of Borough Hall. Bring chairs and blankets, and enjoy the music that will include an evening of marches, popular patriotic songs and light classics under the baton of music director Anthony LaGruth. Meet the grand marshals – Marcia, Walter and Daniel Perry - of the July 4 parade as well. The IDA raffle drawing will take place during the intermission, with prizes including a $500 Visa gift card and a $250 Shop the Rock basket of gift cards from town merchants. Tickets will be available for purchase at Kilroy’s prior to the concert or at Borough Hall that night. Hours: Concert begins at 7 p.m. Go: Borough Hall, 1 Harding Plaza, Glen Rock.
  • Essex County Summer Concert Series and Fireworks. Listen to the Infernos at Brookdale Park and enjoy a fireworks show. The Infernos’ repertoire includes big band, oldies, Motown and today’s chart hits. Founded by the late Bobby Wells, former musical director of the Duprees, the band features lead singer Kenny Simmons, formerly of the Commodores. Hours: Starts at 7:30 p.m. Go: 473 Watchung Ave., Bloomfield.

July 4

  • Ridgefield Park July 4th Celebration. Ridgefield Park will have festivities all day on July 4th, including a reading of the Declaration of Independence, a flag raising ceremony and a parade. Hours: Starts at 7:30 a.m. Go: Memorial Plaza 554 Shaler Blvd., Ridgefield Park.
  • Florham Park July 4th Celebration. During this full day of celebration on July 4, there will be a flag raising ceremony at the Florham Park Fire Department at 315 Brooklake Road, followed by the annual town parade. Then, rides, food, games and more will be available at Emmett Park Field, with fireworks in the evening. Hours: 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Go: Emmett Park Field, 111 Ridgedale Ave., Florham Park.
  • Livingston July 4th Community Celebration. This all-day event on July 4 will feature a car show, food trucks, games, live entertainment and a beer garden. The celebration will conclude with Livingston's annual fireworks show. Hours: 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Go: Memorial Oval, Robert H. Harp Drive, Livingston.
  • Paramus Independence Day Parade. The annual Independence Day Parade in Paramus will feature participates like local first responders, community organizations and more. title: Fourth of July local fireworks shows list for 2024 in North Jersey
fullText:
Independence Day will be here before we know it, so it's time to start planning how you'd like to celebrate. And, while attending a family gathering or a backyard barbecue could be fun, there's nothing quite like ringing in the Fourth of July with some fireworks, parades, festivals and more.

Because North Jersey has celebrations taking place in every corner of the region, we've compiled a list of the currently scheduled events to make your life easier.

And you won't want to miss the the 48th Annual Macy's Fourth of July Fireworks. While this event is technically in New York City, the Macy's July 4th fireworks will take place on the Hudson River for the first time since 2013, meaning New Jersey residents can view them from places like Hoboken, Jersey City and Weehawken. The show begins at 8 p.m.

Here's a look at the Fourth of July events and firework shows taking place across North Jersey in 2024, by location.

Want to see them filtered by date? Head on over to our other story: When are North Jersey fireworks?

Bergen County

Cresskill

4th of July Townwide Celebration. On July 4 (rain date July 5), enjoy a day of fun, food, rides, games, a D.J. and more. Call the Recreation Office at 201-816-8065 or jmitchell@cresskillboro.org for information. Cresskill residents only. Hours: 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Go: Community Center, 100 Third St.

East Rutherford

Meadowlands Fireworks & Fan Appreciation Night. At Fan Appreciation Night at Meadowlands Racetrack on July 6you enjoy $1 concession items, $2 Bud and Bud Light drafts, as well as a free fireworks show for July 4th after the races. Hours: 6 to 11:30 p.m. Go: Meadowlands Racetrack, 1 Racetrack Drive, East Rutherford.

Edgewater

Independence Day Fireworks. Fireworks, live music, food trucks and kids activities on June 27. Bring a chair or blanket. Parking is limited, so attendees are encouraged to use the free River Road shuttle bus. The rain date is June 30. Hours: 6 to 10 p.m. Fireworks begin at approximately 9:20. Go: Veterans Field, 1057-1165 River Road.

Englewood

City of Englewood's Fireworks Show. Mayor Michael Wildes and the Englewood City Council invite you to the City's fireworks celebration on July 1. The rain date is July 2. Hours: 7:30 p.m. Go: Front lawn of Dwight Morrow High School, 274 Knickerbocker Road.

Fair Lawn

Fair Lawn Fireworks Show. Fair Lawn will be hosting their annual fireworks show on June 27. In addition to fireworks, there will be food vendors and live music for guests to enjoy. Tickets for the pre-fireworks festivities are $5 for children under 12 and seniors, $7 for adults and $25 for a family of five. Hours: Gates for the event open at 6:45 p.m., and fireworks begin at sundown. Go: Memorial Park, Berdan Avenue and 1st Street, Fair Lawn.

Glen Rock

Pops Celebrates Nation’s Birthday. The Pops Orchestra goes patriotic on July 3 with a free concert on the lawn of Borough Hall. Bring chairs and blankets, and enjoy the music that will include an evening of marches, popular patriotic songs and light classics under the baton of music director Anthony LaGruth. Meet the grand marshals – Marcia, Walter and Daniel Perry - of the July 4 parade as well. The IDA raffle drawing will take place during the intermission, with prizes including a $500 Visa gift card and a $250 Shop the Rock basket of gift cards from town merchants. Tickets will be available for purchase at Kilroy’s prior to the concert or at Borough Hall that night. Hours: Concert begins at 7 p.m. Go: Borough Hall, 1 Harding Plaza.

Here Comes the Parade on July 4th. Rain or shine, there will be marching bands, pipers, historic Civil War reenactors, floats, clowns and more. For information, write to grparade@icloud.com. Hours: The parade kicks off at 9:30 a.m. Go: The route begins at Glen Rock High School, 400 Hamilton Ave., and goes east on Harristown Road, takes a left on Highland Road, another left at Rock Road through the center of town, and a right on Doremus Avenue, ending at the Municipal Pool parking lot.

Lyndhurst

Lyndhurst's Zappy Fourth of July. At the Lyndhurst Band Shell, there will be a free concert on July 4 with several different performers to celebrate the Fourth of July. Hours: 7:30 to 9 p.m. Go: Lyndhurst Municipal Park, 367 Valley Brook Ave., Lyndhurst.

Paramus

Paramus 4th of July Fireworks Show. Paramus will be hosting their annual Independence Day fireworks show on July 7. Prior to the fireworks show, there will be live entertainment and food vendors. Hours: The time of the event is to be determined. Go: Cliff Gennarelli Sports Complex, Garden State Plaza Parkway, Paramus.

Paramus Independence Day Parade. The annual Independence Day Parade in Paramus on July 4 will feature participates like local first responders, community organizations and more. Hours: Begins at 9 a.m. Go: Starts at the intersection of Farview Avenue and E. Century Road, moving north on Farview Avenue. It will conclude at the Memorial Elementary School on Midland Avenue.

Ridgefield Park

Ridgefield Park July 4th Celebration. Ridgefield Park will have festivities all day on July 4, including a reading of the Declaration of Independence, a flag raising ceremony and a parade. Hours: Starts at 7:30 a.m. Go: Memorial Plaza 554 Shaler Blvd., Ridgefield Park.

Bergen County's Star-Spangled Spectacular. This Independence Day celebration on July 4 will feature the New Jersey Wind Symphony; other live entertainment including the New Jersey Youth Jazz Orchestra, Reggie Pittman Band, Jake Thistle, Leslie Mendelson; children's activities; food trucks; a beer and wine garden; and fireworks at Overpeck Creek. Hours: Starts at 3 p.m. Go: The Amphitheater at Overpeck County Park, Challenger Road, Ridgefield Park. Parking is available in the Ridgefield Park and Henry Hoebel sections of the park, as well as the Glenpointe Alfred Sanzari Building parking garage in Teaneck and the KABR Group parking lots on Challenger Road in Ridgefield Park, with complimentary shuttle transportation.

Ridgewood

Ridgewood 114th Annual Fourth of July Celebration. This all-day event on July 4th features a flag raising at Wilsey Square followed by a parade starting at Monroe Street and Godwin Avenue. Then, there will be evening entertainment, food trucks and a beer garden at Veterans Field, followed by the National Anthem and a fireworks show. Hours: Flag raising begins at 9 a.m.; parade begins at 10 a.m.; evening entertainment begins at 6 p.m.; and the National Anthem and fireworks begin at 9 p.m. Go: Veterans Field, 156-158 Northern Parkway, Ridgewood.

River Edge

River Edge July 4th Parade and Celebration. The events will include a parade on July 4 throughout River Edge, as well as a fair with a variety of vendors. Hours: Starts at 11 a.m. Go: Parade begins on Cherry Hill and ends at Memorial Park on Continental Avenue.

Tenafly

4th of July Celebrations. Rides, food, DJ music and giveaways on June 29, sponsored by the Tenafly Recreation Department. The annual fireworks display will be on July 6, featuring Cyro Baptista's Chama - joyous Brazilian and world music. These events are free for all Tenafly residents. Hours: 10 a.m to 2:30 p.m. June 29 (rain date is June 30). The event on July 6 (rain date July 7) begins at 7:30 p.m. and the fireworks begin at 9. Go: The June 29 event is at Roosevelt Common, behind Tenafly Middle School, 10 Sunset Lane. The July 6 event is behind Tenafly High School, 19 Columbus Drive.

More: Fourth of July events in North Jersey kick off June 26. Here's where to catch them all

Morris County

Denville

Denville's 4th of July Fireworks Celebration. A free concert on July 4 by Street Hassle followed by a fireworks show, presented by the Township. Street Hassle is a horn band that plays classic rock, blues, Motown and pop. Hours: The concert begins at 7 p.m. Go: Gardner Field, 2 Savage Road.

Dover

Dover July 4th Fireworks and Celebration. Dover will be hosting a July 4th celebration with food, activities, live entertainment and fireworks on July 3. Hours: Starts at 6 p.m. Go: 302 E. McFarlan St., Dover.

Florham Park

Florham Park July 4th Celebration. During this full day of celebration on July 4, there will be a flag raising ceremony at the Florham Park Fire Department at 315 Brooklake Road, followed by the annual town parade. Then, rides, food, games and more will be available at Emmett Park Field, with fireworks in the evening. Hours: 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Go: Emmett Park Field, 111 Ridgedale Ave., Florham Park.

Hanover

Hanover Township Patriotic Celebration. Hanover Township is holding their 2024 Patriotic Celebration, which will feature food trucks, live music, games, face painting, balloon art and fireworks. Hours: 6 to 10 p.m. Go: Hanover Township Municipal Complex, 1000 Route 10, Whippany.

Lake Hopatcong

Lake Hopatcong Annual Fourth of July Fireworks. The Lake Hopatcong Yacht Club will be hosting their annual July 4th fireworks on June 28 on the main lake of Lake Hopatcong. Parking will be available on Bertrand Island for residents and members only. Hours: 9:30 to 10:30 p.m. Go: 75 North Bertrand Road, Mount Arlington.

Montville

Montville 4th of July Celebration. From June 26 through June 28, Montville will be hosting their annual 4th of July celebration events. Each day features different attractions, including food and beer trucks, carnival rides, live entertainment, a car show and fireworks. Hours: Open 5 to 10 p.m. each day. Go: Montville Township High School, 100 Horseneck Road, Montville.

Morris Plains

Morris Plains Family Day and Fireworks. The annual Morris Plains Family Day will be held at Morris Plains Community Park on June 29, featuring food, activities and entertainment. Then, their July 4th fireworks show will take place after sundown. Hours: Family Day begins at 5 p.m., and the fireworks begin around 9:30 p.m. Go: 51 Jim Fear Dr., Morris Plains.

Mountain Lakes

Mountain Lakes July 4th Fireworks. A festive July 4th fireworks show will take place July 2 over Mountain Lake, and Island Beach will be open for viewing. Hours: Starts at 9 p.m. Go: 276 Boulevard, Mountain Lakes.

Randolph

Randolph Freedom Festival. Held from July 11 to 13, the Randolph Freedom Festival will feature live music, games, food, a beer garden and fireworks. Hours: 6 to 11 p.m. Go: 214 Center Grove Road, Randolph.

Rockaway Borough

Rockaway Boro Family Festival 2024. The Borough's 47th year with Garden State Fireworks will feature food trucks, a beer truck (age 21 and older with ID), live music by Back to Rock and Street Hassle. and 50/50 raffles to support the RBFD. The rain date is July 7. Hours: The event begins at 4 p.m. with Bach to Rock performing until 6 p.m. Street Hassle performs from 7 to 9:30. The winning raffle tickets will be drawn at 9:30. The fireworks will follow. Go: Fireman's Field, 144 Beach St.

Passaic County

Bloomingdale

Bloomingdale July 4th Fireworks. Bloomingdale will host their annual July 4th fireworks show on June 29 at Walter T. Bergen School. The event will also feature food and rides. Hours: Starts at 6 p.m. Go: 225 Glenwild Ave., Bloomingdale.

Clifton

Clifton Independence Day Celebration. The event on July 6 will feature a festival with food vendors, activities, games, rides, music and more, followed by a fireworks show. Hours: Starts at 4 p.m. Go: 350 Piaget Ave., Clifton.

Paterson

Paterson Food Truck Festival and Fireworks. Visitors are invited to enjoy food from local businesses, as well as a fireworks display, on June 30. Hours: Starts at 5 p.m. Go: Great Falls Welcome Center, 65 McBride Ave. Extension.

Sussex County

Augusta

July 4th Hometown Heroes Parade and Sussex County Miners Game. In Augusta on July 4, events include the Hometown Heroes Parade, a game between the Sussex County Miners and the New Jersey Jackals, as well as a fireworks display. Hours: Starts at 4:30 p.m. Go: 94 Championship Place, Augusta.

Montague

Montague Day and July 4th Fireworks. Montague Day on June 29 will feature the Miss Montague Contest, an animal exhibit, live entertainment, a cornhole tournament, a dunk tank, vendors, food, fireworks after dark and more. Hours: The event starts at 4 p.m., and the fireworks begin after dark. Go: Montague Town Hall, 227 Clover Road, Montague.

Essex County

Belleville

Belleville Fireworks 2024. Mayor Michael Melham and the Township Council present this event on July 3, with fireworks, family fun, face painting, food trucks, clowns, rides and a DJ. Hours: Festivities begin at 6 p.m., fireworks begin at dusk. Go: Belleville Municipal Stadium, 100 Passaic Ave.

Bloomfield

Essex County Summer Concert Series and Fireworks. Listen to the Infernos at Brookdale Park, and enjoy a fireworks show, on July 3. The Infernos’ repertoire includes big band, oldies, Motown and today’s chart hits. Founded by the late Bobby Wells, former musical director of the Duprees, the band features lead singer Kenny Simmons, formerly of the Commodores. Hours: Starts at 7:30 p.m. Go: 473 Watchung Ave., Bloomfield.

Cedar Grove

Cedar Grove Annual Fireworks Display. Cedar Grove is hosting their annual Fourth of July fireworks display and celebration event July 1, which features a live DJ, a balloon artist, a patriotic obstacle course, crafts and refreshments. Hours: Starts at 7 p.m. Go: Panther Park Field, 118 W Bradford Ave., Cedar Grove.

Livingston

Livingston July 4th Community Celebration. This all-day event on July 4 will feature a car show, food trucks, games, live entertainment and a beer garden. The celebration will conclude with Livingston's annual fireworks show. Hours: 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Go: Memorial Oval, Robert H. Harp Drive, Livingston.

Montclair

Montclair July 4th celebrations. The series of celebrations taking place in Montclair on July 4th include the town's 68th annual July 4th parade, followed by a festival in Edgemont Park. Hours: Parade begins at 11 a.m., followed by the family picnic. Go: Parade begins at South Fullerton Avenue and Bloomfield Avenue and travels to Edgemont Park; Edgemont Park, Valley Road and Holland Terrace, Montclair.

Newark

The Essex County Free Summer Concert Series will include two free performances in Newark featuring fireworks displays. Hours: Both concerts begin at 7:30 p.m.

title: Montclair NJ bar chosen by Zach Bryan to preview new album
fullText:
A Montclair bar is set to play unreleased music from country star Zach Bryan — and may even get a visit from the singer himself — prior to his new album next month.

Irish gastropub Egan & Sons was identified by Bryan on his Instagram page as one of 23 bars in the United States and Canada "that embody the spirit of American culture." Starting Monday, each establishment will get a 10-day sneak preview of Bryan's album "The Great American Bar Scene" before its release, fittingly, on July 4.

"My intent with all this is to give everyone an early glimpse of this album," Bryan said, "but more importantly this is in the spirit of bringing people together for a memorable moment."

The full bar list announced Thursday includes one other New Jersey location: Barnacle Bill's in Rumson. The eateries are spread across 15 states, including four in Bryan's native Oklahoma, along with one in Toronto, Canada.

"As much as I'd kill to play all these timeless bars, it won't be possible," Bryan wrote. However, he added, "I will be visiting a few off the list to have a drink with ya'll."

Related: Watch Mets star Pete Alonso dance and sing on stage with country singer Zach Bryan

Egan & Sons shared the news on its own Instagram post and urged residents to stay tuned for updates on the album reveal. The pub clarified that the event is not a concert, but rather a preview of "The Great American Bar Scene."

In another post Friday afternoon, Egan & Sons said its plan is to divide the album into sections and play tracks at regular intervals throughout each night beginning Monday. At the end of the week, either Thursday or Friday weather permitting, the restaurant will host an outdoor listening party and play the full album "as many times as people want to hear it."

The pub will also have a limited amount of Bryan merchandise to distribute to patrons during the week. It is unknown whether the singer will make an appearance, the post stated, but "while we're not making any promises, our fingers are just as crossed as yours."

Bryan, 28, has already released one song called "Pink Skies" off the upcoming album, the fifth in his discography.

The singer has already been recognized with several accolades in his young career. He received the Academy of Country Music Award for New Male Artist of the Year in 2023 and this year's Grammy Award for Best Country Duo/Group Performance for the song "I Remember Everything" featuring Kacey Musgraves.

title: Trendy 14 ounce Stanley tumblers for toddlers
fullText:
The trendy Stanley tumbler has made its way into the kid's cup section of Target and parents on TikTok are loving it.

Earlier this month, lifestyle vlogger Madilynn Cameron, @themadivlog on TikTok, posted a video to her page that said, "This is not a drill. Baby Stanleys for toddlers at Target," with the caption, "Ur coming home with me, Target I'm screaming."

In the video, she highlights small Stanley tumblers that she found on the kid's cup shelves at her local Target.

"They make kids' Stanleys now," she says in the video while picking up the cup in four different colors. "This is the cutest thing ever."

This video, which was posted on June 13, now has over 33,000 likes, 475 comments, and 570,000 views.

More trending: Pocono pair left baby on Lake George Beach. What we know

The cups shown in the video are in fact the 14-ounce version of the Quencher H2.0 Flowstate Tumbler, the same cup that has caused a craze over the last year, rising to the top of the reusable water bottle game. These tumblers have sold out immediately upon dropping online and in stores with some collections being resold for way more than the original price.

The Quencher comes in five sizes including 14, 20, 30, 40 and 64 ounces.

"Compact without compromise, our smallest and lightest Quencher H2.0 is a great choice for quick and easy sipping, wherever the day takes you," says the 14 ounce Quencher's description. "The 14oz size is also perfect for kids, encouraging them to stay hydrated at home, school or the playground."

While these, Stanley's smallest tumblers, have been around for a while, the cups shown in the video appear to be part of the company's brand-new Heat Wave Collection which dropped on June 11.

The 14 ounce Quenchers sold under the Heat Wave Collection can be purchased in four colors including Vivid Violet, Bright Lime, Tropical Teal and Passion Pink.

The 14 ounce Tumbler retails for $20 online and in stores.

Is it Rutt's Hutt in Clifton, where you can indulge in fries smothered in gravy alongside one of its famous rippers?

Maybe it is Davey's Irish Pub and Restaurant in Montvale, where you can choose among shoestring, seasoned waffle, steak, beer battered, or sweet potato fries.

You can go for a classic, crinkle-cut fry, seasoned to perfection at Ted's North Delicatessen in Paramus, or check out Fire and Oak in Montvale where you can order truffle fries topped with a fluffy pile of parmesan cheese.

Whether you like your fries simple and crispy, smothered in toppings, or dipped in a delicious sauce, there are so many options in North Jersey to choose from. Let's crown a winner!

title: Greenwood Lake Airshow 2024 schedule expands for Father's Day
fullText:
The annual Greenwood Lake Airshow is back and expected to be bigger than ever, with an expanded lineup of aerial acrobatics for its nighttime show.

The event takes place this Father's Day weekend, June 14-16, with three day-into-night performances at the airport in West Milford.

"The top performers of the nation are coming here," said Tim Wagner, the air show's chairman. "We are expecting up to 50,000 people."

The event turns 15 this year, with three golds in the International Council of Airshows Pinnacle Awards under its belt. North Jersey's only air show, will feature eight headliners doing stunts involving pyrotechnics and skywriting.

What's new for 2024?

"We started a few years back trying different things out," Wagner said. "Now we have a laser show, an expanded night show and more performers."

Friday's show will honor all of the armed forces in celebration of Flag Day. Four performances will feature retired U.S. military aircrafts, or "war birds." Visitors are encouraged to wear red, white, and blue. Sunday's show will feature a "special skywriting surprise for Father's Day" Wagner told NorthJersey.com.

The event will offer a variety of food options, vendors, and "upgradeable viewing experiences," according to its website. Organizers also recommend general admission visitors bring folding chairs or blankets.

"The war birds are always a favorite," Wagner said. "We have people that leave saying that's the best pyrotechnics they've ever seen."

Greenwood Lake Airshow schedule, tickets

  • Gates open at 4 p.m. Friday with the show beginning at 7 p.m. Gates open at 2 p.m. Saturday and Sunday with performances starting at 5:30 p.m. All shows are expected to end around 9:30 p.m.
  • General admission tickets are $35 per adult, $25 for senior citizens and veterans and $15 per child when purchased online, $5 more at the gate. A family package is $90, granting admission for two adults and up to four children. Other options include the front-line seating package and V.I.P pavilion performer package.

Tickets are available at njairshow.com.According to the show's latest news release, this year's headline acts will include:

  • Spotlight on the Titan Aerobatic Team: The most sought-after civilian aerial act in the industry, these four pilots perform awe-inspiring maneuvers in their World War II T-6 Texans.
  • Nathan Hammond "Ghost Writer": After dark, watch as Hammond lights up the sky with 200 pounds of pyrotechnics and 4,000 brilliant LED lights in a graceful ballet among the stars. 
  • Buck Roetman's High-Energy Aerobatics: Experience the electrifying aerobatics of Buck Roetman, known for his powerful performances with a 375+ horsepower Lycoming engine that fills the sky with roaring sounds and dramatic smoke trails. 
  • Rob Holland, Premier Aerobatic Pilot: Witness Rob Holland, a premier freestyle aerobatic pilot, as he blends precision, artistry, and adrenaline into each routine, captivating spectators with his flawless execution of complex maneuvers.
  • Jerry McCart "The Homewrecker": Be amazed as McCart's 375 mph triple engine jet-powered semi-truck roars down the runway with over 36,000 horsepower.
  • Bob Carlton Makes Debut with Unique Fox Jet Sailplane: Experience Bob Carlton's thrilling debut, where he pilots the unique Fox Jet sailplane, the only two-seater designed for low-level, jet-powered performances, equipped with two PBS TJ-100 jet engines.
  • Airythmia: A Spectacle of Freedom and Fire: Join Airythmia at the Day and Night Show to experience the "irregular" side of aviation with paramotors, featuring a dazzling pyrotechnic display that adds fiery excitement to their celebration of aerial freedom.
  • Experience the Thrill of History: Witness the iconic P-40 Warhawk and P-51 Mustang as they dominate the skies in a breathtaking display of World War II aviation prowess.
seoTitle: Greenwood Lake Airshow 2024 schedule expands for Father's Day
